item.title: Noir-CKB update: what I decided after the direction check, what you can try today, and where this is going
item.dc:creator: xiaomao
item.description:
About a month ago I shared a direction check here for noir-ckb, asking for feedback on what I was building. I got really thoughtful replies, mostly around two questions:

Where should a proof live in a CKB transaction (Lock or Type?), and is Noir → Groth16 even the right backend, given its per-circuit trusted setup.

This post is the follow-up: what I decided, what exists now that you can actually run (including on testnet), and the longer-term picture of where I want this to go. It’s a long one, sorry in advance

Quick recap, if you’re new to this

noir-ckb lets you write a rule in Noir, prove it off-chain, and have a CKB script verify the proof. The sentence that has driven the whole project is:

> A proof that verifies is not the same as a proof that authorizes this Cell transition.

A Groth16 proof can be mathematically perfect and still be about the wrong thing: the wrong Cell, the wrong state change, the wrong network. So the interesting work isn’t only verifying proofs on CKB-VM, it’s binding each proof to the exact transaction it’s attached to, so that a valid proof can’t be reused anywhere else.

Decision 1: where the proof lives

In my reply in that thread I ended up with four possible patterns:

  1. Proof-only Lock for a stateless cell: having a valid proof is the permission to spend.

  2. Generic verifier Lock + binding Type: the Lock checks the proof, the Type checks the proof is about this exact transition. (My earlier Capsule prototype.)

  3. Normal ownership Lock + proof-verifying Type: a signature decides who can spend; the Type verifies the proof and binds it to the state change.

  4. Two proofs, one in the Lock and one in the Type, tied together by shared context.

Where they ended up:

Pattern 3 is now live on testnet, as a small owned counter. A normal secp256k1 Lock controls who may spend the Cell. The counter’s Type Script rebuilds the expected public statement from the actual transaction (network, the consumed Cell, old and new value, successor Lock and capacity) and only then verifies the Groth16 proof. A perfectly valid proof for a different Cell, a different change or a different network gets rejected. The local test suite throws 48 of those attacks at it in CKB-VM, plus three deliberately broken contracts that the tests have to catch.

I’ll be honest about the counter, though: its proof is redundant. Every input is public, so the Type could just check `new = old + 1` itself in a few instructions instead of about 111 million cycles. It proves the plumbing and the binding work. It doesn’t show why you’d want zero knowledge.

So the next example is a stateful version of pattern 1:
A private tally. The Cell holds a commitment to a hidden 64-bit number. Whoever knows a secret key can add a hidden amount (including zero, so an update doesn’t even reveal whether anything was added). There’s no signature: the proof is the permission, and the logic lives in a Type so the state survives each update.

That’s where binding stops being a nice-to-have and becomes the entire security model. With no signature, a proof copied out of the mempool is the only thing between an attacker and your tally, so it has to commit to one consumed Cell, one old and new commitment, one successor and one network. Then it’s useless anywhere else.

What it won’t hide, to be upfront: updates to one Cell are still linkable to each other, and the number of updates, their timing and who paid the fee are public. Fully unlinkable updates would need a shielded pool, which is a different design.

The design is written and accepted, not built yet. Before committing to it I checked the risky parts against the current backend: the hash library that works with my compiler version has a known bug for longer inputs, so every hash in the design takes three inputs or fewer, and a differential test (Noir’s own execution vs. the backend’s constraint system) agreed on all 19 cases I threw at it.

Patterns 2 and 4 are parked for now. I’d rather build them when a real application needs them.

Decision 2: staying with Noir → Groth16 (for now)

It was suggested that I look at the optimized SP1 verifier for CKB-VM, because SP1’s PLONK setup is universal, so no per-circuit ceremony. I took that seriously: I reproduced its verification on CKB-VM (about 66M cycles for the upstream fixture) and a set of rejection cases. It works.

The problem is one step earlier. SP1 proves programs compiled for its zkVM; it doesn’t take Noir circuits. Keeping Noir would mean building a Noir-to-SP1 bridge first (for example, running an ACIR interpreter inside SP1), which I couldn’t find and which would be a whole project on its own. Rewriting circuits in Rust would mean dropping the Noir workflow this project exists for.

So I’m staying with Noir → Groth16 and paying the setup cost properly, with a ceremony (more below). That’s a scoping decision, not a verdict that SP1 is worse. If a Noir path to SP1 appears, the binding layer is the part I’d expect to carry over.

What you can try today

Everything is in one guide: noir-ckb-verifier/docs/try-the-counter.md at main · wamimi/noir-ckb-verifier · GitHub

Part 1, locally, no wallet, no money. One command compiles the circuit, generates a fresh proof, starts a throwaway CKB chain on your computer, and sends real signed transactions that deploy the contract, create a counter and update it with the proof. It runs on Apple Silicon Macs and Ubuntu 24.04 (x86_64 and ARM64), natively or in a container. (Intel Macs and Windows aren’t supported yet.)

Part 2, your own counter on testnet. You don’t deploy anything: the contract and verification key are already on testnet and the proving files are published, so it costs about 262 testnet CKB from the faucet (200 stay locked in your counter, because this demo contract has no withdraw). Before you sign anything, the tool checks that the published files are exactly what’s deployed, that the code on testnet matches them byte for byte, and that your own machine compiles the circuit to the same thing. Then you review, sign and send each transaction yourself with your own `ckb-cli` account. The proof is generated on your machine.

I went through it from a brand new account:

- created at 0: [0x0b6efcd7…888798c](https://testnet.explorer.nervos.org/transaction/0x0b6efcd70f111afd1c885557c84f7b93ef4ee8401dd9fe258b9fb677c888798c)

- updated 0 → 1 with a proof made on my laptop: [0xe6589170…0089126f](https://testnet.explorer.nervos.org/transaction/0xe6589170381a02a249c37be8ab279e6229e2feb8f177f3d572bc63f30089126f)

Doing it as a “stranger” found a couple of rough edges that I fixed straight away. I’m sure you’ll find more, and I’d love to hear about them.

The trust part, plainly

The counter’s keys came from a single-party development setup, made by me. In principle that means I could forge counter proofs. For the counter it’s tolerable, because every update also needs your signature, so nobody can change your counter without your key.

For the private tally it’s not tolerable, since the proof is the only authority. So before the tally goes to testnet I’ll run a small public setup ceremony. It’s a relay where each person downloads the latest file, runs one `snarkjs` command on their laptop (around ten minutes), and posts the hash it prints. If even one contributor throws away their randomness, nobody can forge proofs. A future CKB block hash gets mixed in at the end so nobody can steer the result, and anyone can verify the whole transcript afterwards.

I’m looking for around five contributors(or more) If you’d like to be one, reply here or DM me and I’ll send instructions once the circuit is frozen. (It’s for a testnet developer preview, not an audited production ceremony.)

## Where I want this to go

This is the part I’m most excited about. The developer experience I’m working toward:

> You start a project, bring a supported Noir circuit, declare how its public values map to your Cells, and the tool builds the artifacts, the Type Script and an adversarial test suite for you. You test it locally, deploy to testnet, and connect it to your frontend, where your users generate proofs in their own browser and authorize updates with their own wallet.

Almost none of that exists yet beyond the counter, so here is how I’m thinking about getting there, step by step:

1. A real developer toolkit, natively. Turn today’s reference workflow into an installable CLI that works outside this repository, with clear diagnostics and an explicit list of what’s supported. Then support a project within one well-defined pattern (one owner-controlled Cell transitioning to one successor): a config file for how your public values map to Cell state, early and clear errors when a circuit uses something the backend doesn’t support, and artifact manifests so you can always tell which circuit, key, contract and toolchain belong together. A second small example should build from its own folder without touching toolkit code; that’s the real test of reuse.

2. Proving in the browser, with a wallet. This is where it gets fun, and also where I want to be careful. NoirJS can execute a circuit in the browser and produce a witness, but my route also needs the witness converted to the backend’s layout and a Groth16 proof from snarkjs. Barretenberg’s browser prover (UltraHonk) is a different proof system, so it can’t just be plugged into the existing CKB verifier. So the first milestone is narrow: a proof generated in a browser for the fixed counter must pass the existing on-chain verifier, and altered statements must still be rejected. Phone performance has to be measured as well. If that works, the acceptance app is a little visitor-owned counter: connect a wallet, create your counter, click increment, prove in the browser, sign, see it confirmed.

3. Applications that push the toolkit. Battleship is the one I keep coming back to (and it’s why pattern 3 matters: the player’s Lock authorizes the move, the Type proves the hit/miss answer is consistent with the committed board). But a proof of one move doesn’t make a fair game by itself: turns, timeouts, repeated shots and endings all need their own design. So it’ll be its own project once the architecture holds up.

4. Grow from real demand. More circuit operations, structured inputs, other wallet locks, multi-Cell patterns: added when an actual application needs them, each with its own compatibility statement and attack tests. Production readiness (a real setup strategy, independent review, upgrade policy) is a separate undertaking from a testnet release, and I won’t blur the two.

## What would help most

Try it and tell me where you got stuck and on which OS: Sign in to GitHub · GitHub (never share wallet folders or passwords, just the error and the manifest file).

If you’re building on CKB: what would you want to prove inside a transaction? Which public values would have to match your Cells? Which of the four patterns fits?

Ceremony: reply if you’d like to contribute.

Browser proving: if you’ve tried NoirJS, snarkjs or wallet signing in a CKB frontend, I’d really like to hear what hurt.

Honestly, this has become one of my favourite things to work on. Each week I understand CKB a little better, and every time something breaks on someone else’s machine, the project gets more real. Thank you to everyone who replied to the direction check: it changed what I built. I’m excited to see where this goes, and I’d love for some of you to come along

item.title: POI: Proof of Identity, a platformer on CKB testnet that teaches .cell names by using them
item.dc:creator: LusoCryptoLabs
item.description:
A follow-up to the introduction on Scryve, with the technical side: what each floor does on chain, how the game is built, how the town works, and how to join its first wave.

Play: poi.cellula.id (CKB testnet, free, phone or computer)

What it is, in one paragraph

POI is a short browser platformer built to teach identity on CKB to people who will never read documentation. The player wakes up as a number in the Registry’s tower and climbs to the top to win back a name. Along the way they get a wallet, receive testnet CKB, read a real .cell name, pay by name, verify signed words against the chain, meet post-quantum ownership, register a .cell name of their own with commit-reveal, and sign their first statement with it. Nothing is simulated: every one of those steps is a real testnet operation through CCC and the Cells protocol behind cellula.id.

The design rule throughout is show, don’t tell: a concept is something the player does or watches happen in the world, and words only label what was just seen.

Stack

  • Client: Vite, TypeScript and Pixi.js 8. Every character, Clerk, room and prop is drawn in code with one hand-drawn ink style, so a hero is a rig of baked parts posed every frame (legs solved from where the feet should be, springs for squash, lean and bounce).
  • Rules: the game’s rules (run.ts) are deterministic and separate from drawing, so they are tested headless. Each floor is played by bots of different skill, and the clumsy one, which misses its jump timing by up to 0.16 s, has to reach the door. The test suite is 232 tests.
  • Server: Fastify. It relays the testnet faucet, keeps the board of names and the medals, runs the town’s hub, verifies signed statements on testnet and reads on-chain payments for the shop.
  • Chain: CCC for wallets, transactions and signatures; cellula-sdk (CellsClient, verifyStatement) for names.

What each floor does on chain

1. Intake

No chain here. The server hands out an arrival number per device, and a short game booth makes the point the rest of the game builds on: in a wall of near-identical numbers your own is hard to find, and a name is not.

2. Keys

The key machine opens CCC’s wallet list (JoyID passkey, MetaMask, OKX, UniSat, Khie and the rest), or offers a practice key that never touches the chain. The answer is shown as a door with the wallet’s address on its plate and a key beside it: the address is public, the key stays in the wallet. With a key, the floor’s locked cells open. Then the floor’s boss, Key Support, asks for the twelve words. Reading them to him ends the floor.

3. The fountain

“Fill my wallet” asks the testnet faucet for 10,000 CKB through the game’s server (the faucet’s CORS admits no browser). While the claim travels, the floor keeps playing, and the stairs door opens once the page reads the new balance on chain through CCC (polled every 4 s). Measured on the dev build: the faucet answers in about 1 s and the coins are readable on chain about 25 s later.

4. The archive

The player reaches a desk where a real name is cut open: maria.cell, read live with CellsClient.getAccount() when the player arrives. Four bands show its owner, its manager, its records by kind, and its expiry, each with its value from the chain.

Then pay by name, shown before anything is asked: a wallet is told Pay to: maria.cell, the name’s CKB record (address.309) answers with the address, and coins fly there in the scene. “Try it: send 100 CKB” makes it real: one output to that address, the wallet’s cells as inputs, the fee at 1,000 shannons per KB. Money only goes where the chain said just now; a copy kept in the page is never paid to.

5. The post room

Letters arrive signed by maria.cell, in the cells.statement.v1 format. “Check the seal” runs verifyStatement and shows what it looked at, one row at a time: who owns the name now, whether the seal fits these exact words, and whether the key on the seal is the owner’s. One of the two letters was changed after signing, so its seal cracks on the words, and following it leads to a trap.

The floor’s boss, the Impostor, holds up notes in someone else’s name. Standing on the lamp in his room asks the chain about the note, and he stands exposed when it fails. Three rounds, three forgeries: words changed after signing, a key that is not the owner’s, and a look-alike name that is not registered. The game does not know which statements are real; every verdict comes from the chain.

Left to right: the title; floor 4, maria.cell read with getAccount() and cut open; floor 5, a cells.statement.v1 letter checked with verifyStatement.

6. The Machine

A vault inspector reads v3-first-name.cell from testnet: a name owned by a SPHINCS+ lock (post-quantum) and managed by an ordinary key. The scene sets the two keys side by side, a heavy owner key kept offline and a light manager key for everyday edits, and sweeps the Machine’s beam across both: the light one cracks, the heavy one holds. Then the Machine itself fires a beam that cracks ordinary cells and stops at the first quantum vault.

7. The file

The player registers a .cell name of their own, the protocol’s way:

  1. Reserve. The wallet signs a commit that hides the name, with 100 CKB held until the reveal, so nobody watching can take it first.
  2. Wait. The commit must be 60 s old by the chain’s median time, which trails real time, so the wait is about four minutes. The HUD counts it down from the chain’s own clock, and the floor keeps going: the Registry drops Clerks near the player until the name is ready, and the floor’s boss, the Registrar, fights in the meantime.
  3. Register. At the records counter the wallet signs the reveal, publishing the player’s CKB address on the name as a record.

Then the player signs I am <name>.cell. as a statement (no fee) and the game verifies it on chain, the same check as floor 5. A server-side purse sends each new name 100 testnet CKB by its name. On testnet a name needs five characters or more; a year of one is about 4,000 testnet CKB, which the fountain covers.

The end, the board and the medals

The end screen shows the player’s ID card turning from NO RECORD FOUND to RECORD FOUND, and their points. “Put my name on the board” has the name’s owner sign the score as a statement; the server checks the signature and the name’s ownership on testnet before the entry goes on. There is an all-time board and a board for each week (Monday 00:00 UTC to the next).

Eight medals are given by the server only, for what it can check: a signed climb, a climb under ten minutes, houses got through, the giant brought down together, a harvest brought in, a place among the first hundred names on the town’s list, a week in the top ten. Some unlock accessories that are earned and never sold.

Medals can also be written on the name itself. The game seals the list with a secp256k1 key of its own (signing words like Proof of Self medals of sofia.cell on the CKB testnet: climb (2026-10-06), ... Sealed 2026-10-09.), and the name’s owner writes it as a poi.medals record. Anyone can verify it with CCC’s verifyMessageCkbSecp256k1 against the game’s published key, and a record copied to another name or edited by hand does not verify. Since Cells keeps records in the witness, with only their hash in the cell’s data, writing one costs a network fee and occupies no capacity.

Left to right: floor 7’s booth (why reserving and registering are two steps); the end of the climb with the signed board; the medals screen reading the poi.medals record back. (Example names.)

The town

The second chapter is a town of tiles seen from above, where everyone playing meets live. The climb runs on testnet and is free; the town opens to a name registered on mainnet.

The square with four players connected to the hub, and the giant Clerk the server sends when a room has two or more.

  • The door. A player registers a .cell name on mainnet at cellula.id with their own wallet; the game never handles real CKB. On 2026-10-12 a year of a name of five characters or more cost 3,010 CKB, plus 240 CKB held in the name’s cell. At the town’s door the wallet signs, with that name, I am sofia.cell. I climbed POI as sofi4.cell and join the first wave of its town. (a cells.statement.v1, no fee), through a wallet list of its own pointed at mainnet. The server checks it with verifyStatement against a CellsClient on ClientPublicMainnet, read only, checks that the climb named is on the board, and gives the device a key (it keeps only the hash). The key opens the town’s page and the hub; a hub connection without one is not seen and hears nothing.
  • The hub is a WebSocket on the game’s server with rooms of 40. A client sends where it is up to eight times a second (only what changed); the hub broadcasts the room ten times a second, and other players are drawn 0.15 s behind and interpolated.
  • Names in the town are proved, not claimed: “Show my name” has the wallet sign I am <name>.cell, in the city of names (<nonce>). with a nonce bound to the connection, and the hub verifies it on testnet before your name replaces “visitor” over your head.
  • Houses of names. Every name on the town’s list gets a house. Its door leads to a floor generated from the name’s letters (nine segments chosen by the label, deterministic, so the same name is always the same floor, and every one is checked by the bots), in one of six rooms with its own boss and its own board of times, signed the same way as the climb’s.
  • Together. The giant Clerk and the harvest run on the server, so everyone in a room sees the same state: the giant has more hits in it than one player can land before it leaves.
  • The wardrobe. Colours are free. Accessories cost 200 testnet CKB, paid from the wallet to the game’s purse with the item in the output’s data (poi:item:<id>), and the server reads the payment on chain.

What comes next

More of the game will live on chain, and more of the chain will show up in the game. On the list: the cellula wallet as a sign-in option, so a player’s whole climb can happen with the same account they use on cellula.id; quick pay over Fiber, a channel opened from the wallet sheet (20 to 1,000 CKB, through a hosted LSP), then a name paid through its fiber.link record, accessories for 20 CKB and tips of 0.1 CKB at the booths, with no transaction per payment; more heroes with powers; and more of the game’s moments written to the player’s name rather than kept by our server.

Join the first wave

The town’s list is empty: no house has gone up yet. The first hundred real names on it are the first wave.

  1. Play the seven floors at poi.cellula.id and register the game’s name on floor 7 (testnet).
  2. Sign your climb onto the board at the end.
  3. Register your name on mainnet at cellula.id.
  4. Sign at the town’s door with that name.

Your house goes up in the town, and the first hundred get the founder medal (One of the first 100 houses) and the laurel wreath.

Questions, bugs and ideas are welcome in this thread.

item.title: [DIS] CrowdCell: From Testnet Demo to a Crowdfunding Product on CKB | CrowdCell：把 CKB 测试网上的免信任众筹做成产品
item.dc:creator: Ayoub_Lesfer
item.description:
This is a smaller, rescoped version of the first CrowdCell proposal. The audit, the fee model and the mainnet launch are out of this one and will come back as a separate proposal later.

Edited 2026-10-12. Added at no change to the ask: categories and search (M1), creator updates and a Chinese interface (M3), early finalization once the goal is met (M4). The additions are marked “added” in §8 and §9.

2. Summary

CrowdCell is all-or-nothing crowdfunding on CKB where scripts, not a platform, decide where every pledge goes. It is live on testnet at https://crowdcell.vercel.app.

This proposal requests $5,000 USD (payable in CKB) to turn the testnet app into a product people can actually run a campaign on. It stays on testnet and asks for no audit money. It covers five things:

  1. Trustless finalization, rebrand and landing page (already delivered). Since the first proposal, the campaign total moved on-chain so the outcome is verified by the script, the project became CrowdCell, and the site got a proper landing page. All of it is live and can be checked today.
  2. Dashboards and discovery. “My campaigns” for creators and “My pledges” for backers, plus categories and search on the campaign list.
  3. Creator identity. .cell names and Vellum reputation on campaign pages, so a backer sees who is asking for the money and not just a lock hash.
  4. Creator tooling and first real campaigns. Creator updates on campaign pages, shareable campaign pages, a Chinese interface, a creator guide and mobile QA, with a goal of at least three campaigns run by people outside the project.
  5. Keeper tip and early finalization. A small on-chain tip for whoever triggers release or refund, so settlement no longer depends on my bot. And a creator whose campaign has reached its goal can finalize it without waiting for the deadline.
  • Grant Amount Requested: $5,000 USD (payable in CKB)
  • ETA to Completion: about 3 months from approval
  • CKB Wallet or Funding Address: ckb1qrgqep8saj8agswr30pls73hra28ry8jlnlc3ejzh3dl2ju7xxpjxqgqqxdl32chss0tlfyexs6h74ny8cc3vl90dgpt6evj

3. Project Introduction

A creator sets a funding goal in CKB and a deadline. Backers pledge. If the goal is met by the deadline, the funds go to the creator. If it isn’t, every backer is refunded. Nobody holds the money in between: each pledge sits in its own cell, and the lock script on that cell only allows those two exits.

What problem this solves

Kickstarter-style platforms ask you to trust an operator to hold the funds, decide the outcome and pay out. There is no crowdfunding platform on CKB today, and the cell model fits the problem well: a campaign is a cell, a pledge is a cell, and the rules are the scripts guarding them.

Who this is for

CKB builders first. CrowdCell is a launchpad for CKB projects: the people most likely to use it already have a wallet and CKB. Pledging from a Bitcoin wallet through RGB++ comes later, once the launchpad use case is proven.

What changed since the first proposal

The first proposal asked for $15,000 to go to mainnet, with $7,000 of it reserved for an audit. It got 16 likes and no objections, and the feedback I got afterwards was clear: too big a step, too early. Make it a product on testnet first, keep the ask small, and come back for the audit and mainnet when there is usage to point at.

So I kept building and cut the proposal down:

  • Out: the Scalebit audit, the 5% fee with its config cell and treasury, the mainnet deployment and the launch promo. Fees only matter once real money moves, and that code needs the audit anyway.
  • Already done, unfunded: the last on-chain trust gap is closed, the rebrand is live, the landing page is live.
  • In: the things that make it usable as a product, most of them asked for or offered by people in the community (see §8).

Why now

  • The contracts are in their intended shape for testnet. What is missing is product surface, not mechanism.
  • Two other CKB projects are plugging into CrowdCell: Cellula has opened a PR that shows .cell names (CrowdCell#10), and Vellum has offered its reputation SDK. A third, CKB Service Runner, is at the design stage and has used CrowdCell’s settlement as an example of a keeper job. Doing these while they are also building is cheaper than doing them later.
  • Someone outside the project has already created a campaign on the testnet app. Dashboards and a creator guide are what the next ones need.

4. Team & Roles

LESFER Ayoub @RickSoze, solo developer

  • Role: everything. Contracts (Rust + ckb-std), transaction builder and indexer (TypeScript), frontend (Next.js + CCC), deployment and testing.
  • Background: senior full-stack developer based in Bordeaux, France, with 6+ years shipping production systems. Currently enterprise SaaS at eMenuChoice, previously API and infrastructure work at BricoPrive. Prior smart contract experience on the Alephium DEX (Ralph, on Alephium’s stateful UTXO model), where I implemented core DEX functionality including a multi-pool swap router. Thinking in inputs and outputs carried over well to CKB; the cell model and ckb-std were learned on top of that. MSc in Computer Science, Université de Bordeaux.
  • Time commitment: part-time next to a full-time job, about 4-5 hours a week, sustained for 30 weeks of public progress reports (see §13).
  • GitHub: alesfer001 (Ayoub Lesfer) · GitHub · Telegram: @RickSoze · X: @crowdcellckb

5. Current Status

Everything below is live on the CKB testnet and open-source.

  • Full campaign lifecycle on-chain: create, pledge, finalize, release or refund, with a receipt cell for every pledge.
  • Automatic settlement: a finalization bot finalizes campaigns after the deadline and releases or refunds every pledge. Anyone else can trigger the same transactions from the campaign page.
  • Verified outcome: the campaign cell carries the on-chain total, and the campaign script only accepts “Funded” or “Unsuccessful” if it matches total pledged versus goal.
  • Fail-safe: about 180 days after the deadline, any unsettled pledge can be sent back to its backer without the campaign cell.
  • Reviewed: Officeyutong (CKB core dev) reviewed the v1.1 contracts. All 6 findings were fixed and redeployed, and the whole exchange is public (see §13). He reviewed the v1.2 contracts again in October and found 5 more issues, which are open and listed in §6.5.
  • Product: CrowdCell brand, landing page with the trust model spelled out, the app at /app, JoyID and other CCC wallets.
  • On the site today: four labelled demo campaigns (two active, one funded and paid out, one unsuccessful and refunded, both settled by the bot with nobody touching them), plus one campaign created by someone outside the project.

Links: live app · GitHub · project thread

6. Application Design

6.1 Functional Overview

  1. Create. A creator publishes a campaign cell with a goal and a deadline block. Neither can be changed afterwards.
  2. Pledge. A backer locks CKB into a pledge cell. The campaign’s on-chain total goes up in the same transaction, and a receipt cell lands in the backer’s wallet.
  3. Finalize. After the deadline, anyone can finalize the campaign. The script checks the status against the on-chain total.
  4. Settle. Anyone can release each pledge to the creator (if funded) or refund it to its backer (if not). The pledge lock rejects any other destination.

On-chain: all of the above. Off-chain: an indexer that reads the chain and serves the frontend, and the bot, which only submits transactions anyone could submit.

6.2 Architecture & Design

Contracts (Rust, ckb-std), five in total: campaign type, campaign lock, pledge type, pledge lock, receipt type. Campaigns reference them by code hash, so nobody can upgrade them under a live campaign.

Off-chain (TypeScript): transaction builder on the CCC SDK, indexer (Express + SQLite) with the finalization bot inside it, Next.js frontend with the CCC connector.

What this proposal adds:

  • Wallet-aware indexer endpoints and two dashboard pages.
  • Categories and search on the campaign list. The category is part of the campaign’s metadata; search runs in the indexer.
  • Creator updates: short posts on a campaign page, signed by the creator’s wallet and stored by the indexer. Off-chain, so they cost the creator nothing and add no risk to funds.
  • A Chinese interface next to the English one.
  • Name and reputation lookups on campaign pages: .cell names through Cellula, and reputation through the Vellum SDK, which reads claims by the creator’s lock. After a campaign is funded and paid out, CrowdCell issues a crowdcell.campaign-funded.v1 claim to the creator from its own did:ckb.
  • Two contract changes, shipped in one redeploy. The pledge lock lets the transaction that releases or refunds a pledge pay a small flat tip to whoever submitted it. The tip stays inside the 1 CKB fee allowance the lock already has, so the pledged amount is untouched. And the campaign script lets the creator finalize a campaign as “Funded” before the deadline once the on-chain total has reached the goal, with the pledge lock allowing release as soon as the campaign is finalized as “Funded”. Finalizing as “Unsuccessful”, and every refund, still has to wait for the deadline.

6.3 Design Rationale

Testnet first. The mechanism works. What nobody knows yet is whether builders want to run campaigns on it, and that can be found out on testnet for a fraction of the cost of an audit.

Identity through existing CKB projects, not a new system. A backer needs something to judge a creator by. .cell names and Vellum already exist, their authors offered to help, and both integrations are off-chain, so they add no risk to funds.

Reputation from real outcomes. A “campaign funded and paid out” claim is issued only after the payout transaction, with the campaign id, goal, total raised, backer count and payout transaction in the payload. It can be checked against the chain by anyone.

A tip instead of a trusted bot. Today release and refund are permissionless but only my bot has a reason to run them. A small tip gives independent operators a reason, and it is what a keeper network such as the planned CKB Service Runner would need to run CrowdCell as a job.

6.4 Fee Model and Sustainability

Not in this proposal. The design from the first proposal is unchanged (a 5% fee paid by the creator, on successful campaigns only, enforced on-chain and sent to a multisig treasury) and it ships with the mainnet proposal, after an audit. On testnet there is nothing to charge.

Running costs during this proposal are zero: the frontend and indexer are on free tiers, and the bot spends test CKB.

6.5 Security Without an Audit

A fair question from the last round: how is this safe without an audit? Short answer: it is on testnet, with test CKB only, and it will not go to mainnet without one. Until then, this is what stands in for it:

  • External review. Officeyutong’s review of the v1.1 contracts found 2 high and 4 medium issues. All 6 are fixed, and the thread is public.
  • A second external review, still open. In October 2026 Officeyutong read the v1.2 contracts and found 5 issues. I checked each against the code and he is right on all of them. The two that matter most: a pledge’s deadline is not checked against its campaign’s, and a campaign that has expired but is not finalized yet can still take pledges. Together they would let someone push a failed campaign to “Funded” on testnet for the cost of fees. Four of the five are small checks. They ship first, before M1, each with a test that reproduces the attack, and they are not billed to this grant. The fifth (pledges after the deadline) needs a design change, because CKB has no “not after” time lock, and it is delivered with the contract change in M4.
  • Internal trust-boundary review before v1.2, which found 3 medium issues. All fixed in the current contracts.
  • A balance accounting test that follows every CKB through a campaign. It caught 4 fund-routing bugs before the September redeploy. They are closed, and the exploit attempts are kept in the repo as tests that must keep failing.
  • Small surface for funds to go wrong. A pledge has two exits, plus the fail-safe back to the backer. No admin key, no upgradable contracts.
  • The contract changes in M4 (tip, pledge window, early finalization) get the same treatment: unit tests, exploit tests, the accounting test, and a request for review on the PR before it is deployed.

An independent audit is the first line of the mainnet proposal.

7. Key Benefits for CKB

  • A crowdfunding platform on CKB. There isn’t one. A launchpad where CKB projects can raise from the community is useful to the ecosystem on its own.
  • A use case for other CKB projects. .cell names get shown where they matter, Vellum gets a partner issuing reputation from real outcomes, and keeper projects such as Service Runner get a paid job they could run.
  • Activity on-chain. Each campaign brings a creator and its backers, and each one produces creation, pledge, finalization and settlement transactions.
  • A reference for the cell model. Custom locks that route funds by outcome, permissionless finalization, an on-chain accumulator with contention retry. All open-source, with the review and fix history public.
  • A cheap test of demand. $5,000 on testnet tells the community whether the audit and mainnet are worth funding next.

8. Detailed Deliverables & Milestones

Milestone Deliverables ETA Budget
M0: Trustless finalization, rebrand, landing page (delivered) On-chain total and script-verified outcome, trust-boundary and fund-routing fixes, testnet redeploy and end-to-end run with JoyID, CrowdCell rebrand, landing page. Live now, see §5. Done $1,500 (30%)
M1: Dashboards and discovery Wallet-aware indexer endpoints. “My campaigns”: status, raised, backers, and the actions available. “My pledges”: status and outcome of each pledge, receipts, and deposits that can be reclaimed. Added: categories and search on the campaign list. Week 4 $1,200 (24%)
M2: Creator identity .cell names for creators and backers, contributed by Cellula in CrowdCell#10 and extended to the dashboards. Vellum reputation shown on campaign pages and cards. crowdcell.campaign-funded.v1 schema published and the claim issued after payout. Week 7 $900 (18%)
M3: Creator tooling and first real campaigns Campaign pages with link previews for sharing, a creator guide, and mobile QA. Added: creator updates on campaign pages, and a Chinese interface. Goal: at least 3 campaigns on testnet run by people outside the project, with the result reported in this thread. Week 9 $600 (12%)
M4: Keeper tip, pledge window and early finalization Tip on release and refund in the pledge lock, the fix for pledges after the deadline (§6.5), tests, testnet redeploy and end-to-end run, and a standalone keeper script anyone can run. Added: early finalization by the creator once the goal is met. Week 12 $800 (16%)

Total: $5,000 USD, paid in CKB at disbursement. The items marked “added” were added on 2026-10-12 and do not change the total or the dates. M0 is paid on approval since it is already delivered. Each later milestone is paid when it is live on testnet and reported in this thread.

Where each item comes from:

  • Dashboards have been on the roadmap since the MVP and were part of the first proposal.
  • Categories, search, creator updates and early finalization come from the project’s own backlog. They and the Chinese interface were added on 2026-10-12.
  • .cell names were suggested by LusoCryptoLabs (Cellula), who also wrote the first version (CrowdCell#10). The work left for this milestone is the review, names on the dashboards, and moving lookups to the indexer so visitors’ browsers don’t contact a third party.
  • The Vellum schema was worked out with truthixify on the Vellum thread.
  • The keeper tip comes out of the Service Runner thread, where psawyerberlin used CrowdCell’s finalization bot as an example of a keeper job and we discussed what a reasonable tip would be. Service Runner itself has no code yet, so the tip is built to work with any keeper.

The ETA is based on the pace of the last 30 weeks of public progress reports.

9. Budget Breakdown

All of it is development time. There is no audit, no marketing spend and no hosting cost in this proposal.

Milestone Line Amount
M0 On-chain total, verified finalization, fixes, redeploy and end-to-end run $900
M0 CrowdCell rebrand and landing page $600
M1 Wallet-aware indexer endpoints $300
M1 Creator dashboard $450
M1 Backer dashboard $450
M1 Categories and search (added) included
M2 .cell names: review of the Cellula PR, dashboards, indexer-side lookup $250
M2 Vellum reputation display $250
M2 Claim schema and issuance after payout $400
M3 Shareable campaign pages $150
M3 Creator guide $150
M3 Mobile QA and fixes $150
M3 Onboarding the first outside campaigns $150
M3 Creator updates (added) included
M3 Chinese interface (added) included
M4 Pledge lock tip, pledge window fix and tests $450
M4 Early finalization and tests (added) included
M4 Testnet redeploy and end-to-end run $200
M4 Standalone keeper script and docs $150
Total $5,000

10. Out-of-Scope / Future Funding Needs

Not part of this proposal. These are planned for a follow-up proposal once there is testnet usage to show:

  • Independent security audit. Scalebit quoted $5,000 for the v1.1 contracts in June. A firm quote for the final contract set will be attached to that proposal.
  • Fee model and treasury. The 5% creator-side fee, its config cell and the multisig treasury.
  • Mainnet launch. Deployment, bot funding, launch announcement.

Further out:

  • Pledging from a Bitcoin wallet through RGB++.
  • Token, governance and DAO custody of the treasury.

11. Risk & Mitigation

  • Nobody outside the project runs a campaign. M3 depends on other people. One outside campaign already exists, and the creator guide and dashboards are there to lower the bar. If three don’t happen by week 9, I’ll report how many did and what held the others back. M3 is paid for the tooling, the guide and the onboarding work, not for the count.
  • Dependencies on Cellula and Vellum. Both are young projects. The integrations fall back cleanly: no name shows the short hash, and no reputation shows nothing. The keeper tip depends on no other project: it works with any keeper, including my own script, whether or not Service Runner ships.
  • Contract changes without an audit (M4). Testnet only, test CKB only, with the checks listed in §6.5. If review turns up a problem I can’t close in the tip or in early finalization, that change stays off and M4 isn’t claimed.
  • Time. I work on this part-time. The estimate comes from what I’ve actually shipped per week over 30 weeks, not from a plan. The items added on 2026-10-12 are small next to the milestones they sit in, and the dates are unchanged. If one of them slips, I’ll say so in the milestone report.
  • Free-tier hosting. The indexer runs on a free tier and is kept awake by a scheduled ping. Fine for testnet; paid hosting belongs to the mainnet proposal.

12. Closing / Call to Action

The first proposal asked the community to fund a mainnet launch on trust. This one asks for a third of that, a good part of it for work that is already live, and the rest for the things that will show whether CrowdCell gets used.

If you have a project you’d like to run a test campaign for, tell me in this thread and I’ll help you set it up. Questions and pushback are welcome too.

Thanks for reading.

item.title: CellScript Roadmap: Expanding the Frontier of CKB-Native DeFi
item.dc:creator: ArthurZhang
item.description:
I’ve spent the recent CellScript releases working on the less visible parts of contract development: resource ownership, transaction bindings, generated verifiers, build reproducibility, and making sure the compiler’s promises survive actual CKB-VM execution.

As the syntax and core semantics settle down, I am now thinking about to put those foundations to work on a much larger application problem: making advanced, composable DeFi practical to build directly on CKB.

The tentative timeframe is late 2026 to Q1 2027, broadly around the CellScript 0.40–0.50 release series, with the aim of delivering a developer-facing capability set comparable in breadth to that of modern DeFi systems such as Uniswap v4: concentrated liquidity, programmable pool behaviour, custom fees and accounting, and multi-operation settlement.

One principle behind the whole roadmap

DeFi belongs in protocol packages, not in the CellScript compiler.

A Pool, Order, Position, or Hook should be an ordinary type defined by its author. Fees, swap formulas, LP issuance, order pricing and settlement rules are application logic. CellScript’s job is to provide sound ownership rules, checked arithmetic, typed transaction access, precise external Script identities, predictable compilation and usable builders.

This matters on CKB. A transaction can contain multiple independently verified Lock and Type Script groups, but the VM does not offer Ethereum-style synchronous contract calls or shared mutable contract storage. We need to work with the Cell model: verify the whole transaction, bind the actual Cells being spent and created, and make any temporary accounting explicit.

The objective is comparable financial functionality, not EVM bytecode or Solidity compatibility. I would rather ship a CKB-native implementation with clearly documented differences than claim compatibility that only exists in a diagram.

Roadmap at a glance

This is the tree of work. The dependency graph further below shows how the individual issues connect and in what order they can be delivered.

flowchart TB
    ROOT["#43 — Composable finance on CKB"]
    ROOT --> LANG["General language and runtime"]
    ROOT --> BASE["Basic financial protocols"]
    ROOT --> RANGE["Range liquidity and pool execution"]
    ROOT --> ACCOUNT["Multi-operation asset accounting"]
    ROOT --> EXT["Extensible pool behaviour"]
    ROOT --> OBS["Time and price observations"]
    ROOT --> DX["Developer workflows"]
    ROOT --> TEST["Independent evidence"]

    LANG --> L1["#49 Cell selection · #48 Nested ABI · #47 Collections"]
    LANG --> L2["#28 Compatible handles · #29 Open roles"]
    BASE --> B1["#52–#55 Pools, custody, LP, maths, builders"]
    BASE --> B2["#56–#60 Orders, settlement, recovery, reproduction"]
    RANGE --> R1["#61–#65 Pool identity, ticks, positions, cross-tick swaps"]
    ACCOUNT --> A1["#66–#68 Ordered deltas, backed claims, native CKB"]
    EXT --> X1["#69–#71 Hooks, fee policy, custom accounting"]
    OBS --> O1["#72–#73 Time guarantees and historical prices"]
    DX --> D1["#74–#77 Positions, routing, intents, indexers"]
    TEST --> T1["#78–#79 Outside developers and solvency tests"]

There are two distinct kinds of work here. The language/runtime issues help any CellScript application. The FIN issues exercise those capabilities through specific, independently checkable financial protocols. Neither track should quietly absorb the other’s responsibilities.

1. Language and runtime foundations

These are open, general-purpose workstreams. They make complicated transactions easier to express without weakening what an emitted Script actually verifies.

Issue Work Why a DeFi developer would care
#49 — Heterogeneous Cell selection Select and match bounded Cells across different Script identities, with complete input/output correspondence. A swap or batch settlement may touch different assets and independently governed state Cells. The verifier must know which ones are part of the operation and which are unrelated.
#48 — Nested dynamic ABI Canonical, bounded decoding of nested values and variable-length records. Richer batch plans and protocol payloads should not require ad hoc byte parsing or trust a builder’s encoding.
#47 — Bounded collections Deterministic verifier-local Vec, Map and Set support within fixed resource limits. Useful for aggregation, duplicate detection and temporary accounting during a transaction. This is not persistent pool storage.
#28 — Compatible-open handles Select an implementation through a verified interface, artifact and deployment policy. A protocol can admit a compatible external component without trusting a package name alone.
#29 — Open cross-Script roles Bind selected participants and their Script roles into one checked transaction. A pool, token or verifier can be selected at construction time while retaining explicit identity and authority boundaries.

Some of the hardest foundations are already present: bounded Cell lifecycle operations, typed transaction views, exact Script handles and ProtocolBundle give us a starting point. Open issues extend that accepted surface; they do not mean every subsequent application is already supported.

I don’t want to make #47–#49 or #28–#29 mandatory gates for every pool. An exact-deployment pool should be able to ship on its own terms. More general capabilities enter when a concrete transaction needs them.

2. Basic pools, orders and settlement

The first financial milestone is deliberately conventional: a real pool, holding real assets, with verifiable LP accounting. That sounds simple, but there is an important difference between checking a swap formula and protecting the funds behind it.

In the existing examples, a pool action can express reserves, fees and liquidity changes. The new programme requires the full asset lifecycle: a reserve cannot be spent without an authentic matching pool transition, LP shares cannot be forged or destroyed outside their authorised supply rules, and the generated builder must construct a transaction that passes all participating Script groups.

Issues Deliverable
#52 + #53 Authentic custody, asset and LP identities, checked wide arithmetic and independently modelled rounding.
#54 + #55 Complete constant-product pool and LP lifecycle, both trade directions, generated builders and a second pool reproduced by another developer.
#56 + #57 Escrowed orders that support partial fills and cancellation, then settlement against a genuine pool. This is not a complete central-limit-order-book matcher.
#58 Bounded multi-pool routing and separately authenticated shared-payment allocations. Pure pool routing does not depend on the order work.
#59 + #60 Stale-state recovery, contention/cost measurements and independent reproduction using the documented SDK.

One test I care about is intentionally bypassing our own builder. If someone assembles a raw transaction that spends the reserves but omits the pool transition, the on-chain policy should reject it. A successful happy-path transaction isn’t sufficient evidence.

3. Concentrated liquidity: from reserves to price ranges

A constant-product pool treats liquidity as one shared reserve curve. Concentrated liquidity lets a provider allocate liquidity to selected price ranges. That changes the state-management problem substantially: each trade may move through several ranges, and each position earns fees according to where liquidity was active.

Issues Work
#61 Canonical pool identities, permissionless creation for admitted configurations, and reusable state layout.
#62 Tick, square-root-price, liquidity and precisely rounded swap-step mathematics.
#63 Authenticated sparse tick indexes and complete next-boundary proofs.
#64 Range positions, changes in active liquidity, fee growth and donations.
#65 Bounded cross-tick swaps, exact-input and exact-output amounts, price limits and genuine final state.

#63 is an especially interesting CKB problem. Suppose a builder supplies tick 100 and tick 120, but an initialised tick exists at 110. Checking that 100 and 120 are valid Cells doesn’t prove they are the next relevant boundaries. The verifier must also prove the absence of the omitted tick. We need authenticated sparse state, not merely a list supplied by the transaction creator.

A transaction may have a measured upper bound on how many ticks it crosses. That should not turn into an arbitrary cap on how many positions the pool can hold over its lifetime.

4. Multi-operation accounting, claims and native CKB

More complex trading requires accounting for several operations before producing the final transaction outputs. For example, a user might remove liquidity, swap part of the proceeds, then deposit into another position.

There is no reason to model that as an EVM-style nested call stack. On CKB we can validate an ordered logical transition and its final authenticated Cells, provided the intermediate values and obligations are completely checked.

Issues Work
#66 Ordered operation batches with explicit per-user, per-asset debits and credits; all outstanding obligations must settle.
#67 Transferable claims backed by real custody balances, with correct redemption and no double counting. These claims are distinct from LP positions.
#68 Native CKB trading, separating tradeable CKB, occupied Cell capacity, refunds and transaction fees.

The important accounting question is straightforward: who owns each amount before and after the operation, and what backs every claim? A credit belonging to Alice cannot silently pay Bob’s debt. Native CKB kept alive as storage capacity cannot simultaneously be sold as available liquidity.

5. Hooks, fee policy and custom accounting

This is where I want CellScript to become genuinely useful for people building their own market mechanisms.

A hook should be an independently authored protocol component, with declared entry points and permissions. A pool can require it to run before or after selected operations. Its actual result must be bound to the correct operation and checked on chain. Merely recording a hook’s code hash is not evidence that the hook executed.

Issues Work
#69 Authenticated before/after lifecycle hooks, executable return-value contracts and strict permissions.
#70 Separate LP fees, protocol fees, dynamic fee updates and extension charges, with clear ownership and authority.
#71 Permissioned balance adjustments and alternative pricing curves, subject to complete asset settlement.

CKB Script groups validate a transaction independently. They don’t synchronously call one another. Hook execution and logical order need their own enforceable design, potentially using exact external verifier execution and authenticated state transitions. That’s one of the first interfaces I want to prototype rather than leave as a promise at the end.

I’m particularly interested in what an outside developer can do with this: a custom fee model, a permissioned liquidity pool, a different pricing curve, or a protocol that issues a persistent order instead of completing an immediate swap. Those examples should be possible without editing the compiler.

6. Time, observations and the developer experience

A sophisticated pool also needs reliable historical data and a practical way for users to interact with positions.

Issues Work
#72 Establish which expiry, time and freshness claims are genuinely enforceable under CKB’s available chain context.
#73 Optional authenticated price observations and time-weighted queries, with explicit missing-history and stale-data handling.
#74 Position creation, updates, transfers, fee collection and non-custodial subscriptions.
#75 Bounded command plans for swaps, liquidity changes, settlement and authorised migrations.
#76 Scoped signed intents, delegation, nonces, revocation and replay protection.
#77 State indexing, extension-aware quotes, route discovery and generated client workflows.

Time is one area where we have to be careful. A historical header isn’t necessarily proof of the current time, and a wallet timeout is not automatically an on-chain expiration rule. Where the chain cannot enforce an exact guarantee, the SDK needs to say so. The same goes for quoting a pool with an extension whose financial effects the SDK cannot evaluate.

7. What counts as done

There is a difference between a feature compiling, an isolated verifier accepting a fixture, and an application that another developer can use safely.

For this roadmap, I’m looking for three kinds of evidence:

Financial correctness. Real pool reserves and positions must obey their ownership and accounting rules. A malformed transaction should fail even if it bypasses our builder. Cross-tick swaps must not skip a live price boundary. No two obligations may claim the same payment; no claim may be issued without backing; no hook may exceed its declared authority.

Complete transaction execution. The tests must run the relevant Lock and Type Script groups against the same final transaction, with exact executable and CellDep identities. CKB-VM cycles, witness sizes, occupied capacity and the behaviour under contention all matter. Where recovery is needed, the builder must preserve the user’s signed limits rather than silently relax them.

Developer reproducibility. Someone outside the implementation work should be able to instantiate a new pool, manage positions and build at least one meaningful third-party hook from the public packages and generated SDK—without touching CellScript codegen or replacing compiler-generated verifier bytes.

#78 tracks the independent extension work. #79 starts the continuous differential and solvency testing early. These are not ceremonial final checkboxes; they are how we find out whether the earlier layers actually compose.

This also sets an honest limit on the claim. Functional coverage does not prove identical EVM execution, all possible hook behaviour, a completed independent security audit, mainnet readiness or sufficient liquidity. Those require their own evidence and decisions.

item.title: FiberSurvivors: a browser survivors-like for Fiber
item.dc:creator: TranNhi27
item.description:
Hi everyone!

I’ve been working on FiberSurvivors, a top-down survivors-like (kinda like Vampire Survivors) that runs in the browser, where the CKB you earn and the upgrade cards you buy are all paid over Fiber.

So a run goes like this:

  • You open the game and a Fiber node starts in your browser, with its own wallet
  • You fund it from the testnet faucet
  • Press Play, and the game opens a channel to the hub node (game’s reward liquidity)
  • Clear a level, and the hub pays you CKB
  • Buy upgrade cards mid-run by paying an invoice
  • Cash out at the end, the channel closes and your CKB goes back on-chain

All you need is a browser tab, no extension, no local node, no CLI. Everything runs on testnet.

The Loop Graph:

fund a channel ──► fight through 10 levels ──► hub pays each level cleared
                              ▲                             │
                              │                             ▼
                       stronger build ◄──── spend earnings on upgrade cards
                              │
                              ▼
                   cash out ──► channel closes, CKB settles on-chain

So it’s more rewards vs more power. You earn more if you buy fewer cards, kite well and win, but if you lose a level, the run ends there. Right now there are 10 levels with a dragon boss at the end, more might come later.

Motivation

While learning Fiber and CKB, I felt like Fiber fits PvP games best, since two players can pay each other directly over a channel, so you don’t have to put all the trust on one server. But for UX, I wanted players to have a smooth experience without setting up a local node or finding someone to match with, and on a testnet demo it’s pretty hard to find another player online. So in the end it became a single-player game where you earn CKB by playing and spend it on upgrades, at least for now.


Try it

Demo: https://zesty-youtiao-8586ae.netlify.app

SDK repo: Fiber WebGL SDK

The game source isn’t public since it uses some paid assets (Feel and the Vefects Effect Pack), and their licenses don’t allow sharing them. But all the Fiber parts are in the SDK, which is fully open.

How it works

The game is built in Unity (WebGL). For the Fiber part I use my own Fiber WebGL SDK, which runs Fiber’s WASM node (@nervosnetwork/fiber-js) inside the build.

On the other side there’s one fnn node (the hub) on a small cloud VM, plus a small Express server next to it. Every player opens one channel to the hub, and all rewards and card payments go through it.

The server is the one deciding money, not the client:

  • Rewards: The coins you pick up only count once you reach the exit. That’s when the client claims them, the server checks the claim, and the hub pays you. Die before the exit and those coins are gone. The full campaign is 10 levels and pays up to 216 CKB
  • Cards: When you buy a card, the client only sends the card id. The server makes an invoice with the price, then the client decodes it and checks the price matches what it showed you before paying. Cards are 5 to 45 CKB, so if you buy a lot you can actually end a run with less than you started with lol
  • Cash out: Cash out closes the channel and settles both sides on-chain

Each player channel is 400 CKB, and the hub puts in 400 CKB on its side too.

The SDK

While building this I ended up turning all the Fiber stuff into a Unity package, which I submitted to the Gone in 60ms Hackathon where my winning chances were also gone in 60ms

Anyway, any Unity WebGL game can use it too:

  • IPaymentGateway: start the node, connect, open/close channels, keysend
  • IInvoicePaymentGateway: decode an invoice, check the amount, pay
  • IUdtPaymentGateway: xUDT channels and payments, route dry-runs
  • IFiberWallet: on-chain CKB balance
  • IFiberDiagnostics: peers and channels

There’s a sample scene in the repo if you want to try it without the game.

Limitations

Well, to be honest this is a tech demo for “a Fiber node inside a Unity browser game”. The money side is protected: the client never decides an amount, rewards come from the server, and card prices come in server-made invoices. But the gameplay itself isn’t verified

  • You trust the server: The server can’t see the gameplay itself, but it rejects claims that are out of order, too fast, or have more coins than the level could drop. With one claim per level per session and a payout cap per player, that’s what stops reward spamming for now, but there’s no real anti-cheat.

  • The key lives in the browser: Like any Fiber node, it signs automatically, but here the key is kept in the browser’s localStorage for this site. If you clear your site data, the key and any CKB in it are gone. That’s okay for testnet, but letting players back up the key, or binding it to their own CKB wallet, would fix this.

  • Opening a channel takes a few minutes on testnet since it waits for on-chain confirmation.

How to play

There’s a tutorial in the game, but here are the controls:

Controls: WASD to move, attacks are automatic, 1 to 4 to use a skill, left-click to aim, right-click to cancel.

Some tips

  • If the channel open fails, wait a minute and try again, testnet can be slow sometimes
  • Don’t forget to cash out at the end to get your CKB back on-chain

Credits

Kudos to these free assets, they helped me build this a lot faster:

  • KayKit’s Packs for my game including Characters, Skeleton Enemies, Environment, Animations
  • My cute Dragon Boss
  • Space Game GUI Kit
  • 500 Free Skill Icons

Thank you for reading till here, any feedback is welcome

CKB Pulse · Last 7 days

627 updates by 62 people in 58 projects, in the last 7 days.

Every project is a block. When someone pushes code, proposes or reviews a change, reports a problem or publishes a release, a light flies from their face to the project and the block grows. Watch it live, or replay the last 24 hours or the last 7 days in a minute or two. Drag to turn the view, tap a block to open the project.

What you can see

  • Highlights of the day, the week and the month: the most active projects, people and organisations, with medals.
  • Active developers per month over the last two years, and how many committed for the first time.
  • New CKB projects from the last 14 days, flagged when they appear. Follow projects and people on your device and get a notice when they move.
  • For projects with contracts on mainnet: the CKB in cells that use them, transactions and last use, from the CKB explorer and the ckb-cli deployment files the project commits.
  • A picture to share for the highlights, any project or any person.
  • The counters at the top open everything as plain lists, for keyboards and screen readers.

How it finds projects

Nobody keeps the list by hand. Every few hours it searches GitHub for repositories that use CKB libraries (CCC, Lumos, Spore, RGB++, JoyID, ckb-std, the Go and Java SDKs and more) or carry CKB topics. It also checks the other projects of the people working in them, and the repositories behind scripts registered on the CKB explorer. A new organisation appears on its own when it starts working, and leaves after 30 days without work by people.

Missing a project? Add a topic such as ckb or nervos to its repository, or type the GitHub name in the “New” tab, under “Missing someone?”. It joins when GitHub shows public CKB work from the last 30 days.

How it counts

Only work by people. Bots, AI agents working on their own branches (claude/, codex/, copilot/ and others) and the same update pushed day after day by a script show as grey sparks and stay out of the numbers and medals. Merging an agent’s work still counts. For medals, one person counts at most 10 updates per project per hour.

GitHub’s public events arrive 30 seconds to a few hours late, so live means as soon as GitHub tells us.

The code is open, MIT: GitHub - LusoCryptoLabs/ckb-pulse: Live GitHub activity of the CKB ecosystem, drawn in 3D · GitHub

What would you like to see on it, and who is missing?

item.title: Tactus O1: First Based EVM Rollup on CKB
item.dc:creator: ArthurZhang
item.description:
One canonical history. No privileged L2 sequencer.

Following my earlier discussion on based EVM architectures for CKB, I’ve taken this direction forward as an independent project: Tactus O1.

Tactus O1 is an experimental EVM validity rollup designed around CKB’s PoW consensus and Cell model. The central idea is to allow independent builders to propose EVM batches, while CKB determines their canonical succession and eventually verifies the resulting execution through validity proofs.

I’m developing this as a solo research and engineering project for now. The repository already contains working components and reproducible experiments, although the complete rollup and its security guarantees are still under development.

1. The direction

Godwoken established an important precedent for running Ethereum-compatible applications on CKB. With Tactus O1, I’m interested in taking a different approach to sequencing and settlement.

The goal is to combine:

  • Permissionless batch proposals, with CKB rather than a privileged L2 sequencer determining canonical history.
  • Ethereum-compatible execution, built around Reth/revm and familiar Solidity tooling.
  • CKB data availability, so accepted transaction inputs can be independently retrieved and replayed.
  • Validity-enforced settlement, with execution proofs verified on CKB.
  • Independent recovery and exits, without relying indefinitely on the original operator.

The intended architecture is:

flowchart TB
    U["Ethereum wallets and applications"]
    B["Independent batch builders"]
    C["CKB PoW + Cell-based ordering"]
    D["CKB batch-data publication"]
    E["Independent EVM replay"]
    P["ZK validity proving"]
    S["CKB settlement and withdrawals"]

    U --> B
    B --> C
    B --> D
    C --> E
    D --> E
    E -. "Planned" .-> P
    P -. "Planned" .-> S

The important distinction is that builders still determine transaction order within their candidate batches. CKB determines which batch succession becomes canonical.

The proposal therefore removes the need for an exclusive L2 sequencing authority, but it does not automatically eliminate censorship or guarantee fast confirmations.

Those properties need to be established separately.

2. Why O1?

The previous thread explored the broader design space. Here is the short version of where I’ve landed:

Settlement model CKB data availability External data availability
ZK validity O1 — Selected baseline O2 — Future Validium domain
Optimistic O3 — CKB-VM Court research O4 — Parked

I’ve chosen O1: CKB-based sequencing, CKB data availability and ZK validity settlement as the initial development path.

It offers a relatively clear security model: CKB establishes the accepted batch history, the necessary execution data is published on CKB, and validity proofs are intended to secure the resulting state transitions.

External DA may eventually be useful for higher-throughput applications, but it introduces different recovery assumptions. I would rather establish the O1 guarantees first than introduce those assumptions prematurely.

O3 remains an interesting research direction, particularly for CKB-VM-based adjudication, but it is not part of the initial implementation.

3. What exists today?

I’ve been working on the protocol’s basic execution, ordering and recovery boundaries.

The repository now includes:

  • CKB ordering experiments, exercised on isolated CKB devnets with competing transactions and controlled reorganisations.
  • EVM execution and differential tests, comparing a pinned Shanghai-profile revm implementation against Geth on a limited set of workloads.
  • Authenticated batch-data publication, followed by independent EVM state reconstruction from canonical CKB history.
  • Priority-inclusion experiments, testing how CKB Cell dependencies behave under competing and uncooperative builders.

One result has been particularly instructive.

A priority message can be legitimately admitted on CKB, and a challenge against its omission can mature successfully, while a builder continues producing valid batches without processing that message.

flowchart TB
    A["User submits a priority message"]
    B["Message is admitted on CKB"]
    C["Challenge becomes valid"]
    D["Builder continues producing batches"]
    E["Message remains unprocessed"]
    F["Enforceable processing rule"]

    A --> B --> C --> D --> E
    E -. "Still required" .-> F

This illustrates the difference between being allowed to submit a transaction and having an enforceable right to its processing.

It is also why I don’t consider permissionless batch construction alone sufficient evidence of censorship resistance.

The experiments are making progress, but G2 — enforceable forced inclusion — remains open.

4. What comes next?

The immediate objective is to complete one coherent, independently verifiable rollup path:

Ethereum execution → CKB ordering and data publication → validity proof → CKB settlement → independent withdrawal.

There are three main questions I want to resolve:

Enforceable inclusion. Can CKB’s existing Cell and Script primitives require the processing of admitted priority messages without introducing a privileged sequencer or an unacceptable contention bottleneck?

Settlement liveness. How can the protocol ensure that a canonically accepted batch cannot permanently block later settlement because its execution is unprovable?

Independent recovery. Can another operator reconstruct the necessary state and proving inputs, settle valid execution, and support withdrawals after the original operator disappears?

The project has reproducible local evidence for several underlying mechanisms, but not yet for these complete guarantees. End-to-end ZK settlement, production custody and independent exits remain unfinished.

I’m deliberately keeping more elaborate fast-preconfirmation schemes, execution DAGs and external DA outside the initial implementation until the core security path is established.

5. An open invitation

I’ll be introducing Tactus O1 at CKBCon on 13 October 2026.

I’d be particularly interested in feedback from people working on CKB consensus, scripts, transaction propagation, ZK proving and Ethereum execution.

Code, specifications and experiments:

github.com

GitHub - Tactus-Labs/tactus-o1: Tactus O1 — a CKB-based EVM validity rollup:...

Tactus O1 — a CKB-based EVM validity rollup: off-chain-first execution, permissionless CKB-based sequencing, validity-enforced settlement

Tactus is a musical term for a shared beat. I like the analogy for what this project is trying to achieve: independent participants, one canonical history, and no privileged L2 conductor.

CKB Off-Chain Hanoi Event Overview

On 8 October 2026, Nervos Community Catalyst, in collaboration with BPSClub and TexLabs, held CKB Off-Chain Hanoi at Nguyen Trai University’s Faculty of Information Technology & Digital Transformation.

The event brought together CKB developers, other software developers, faculty members and university students. It was an important milestone for the CKBuilders programme in Vietnam, giving local builders an opportunity to present their work, share their experiences and meet one another in person.

Opening the Event

The event was opened by Mr. Trinh Chung, a lecturer at the Faculty of Information Technology & Digital Transformation. He spoke about the importance of blockchain technology and its growing relevance to students and developers.

We were encouraged by his openness towards blockchain and his willingness to provide students with exposure to emerging areas of technology. Our conversations with him also provided a useful starting point for exploring how students and the wider university community might participate in future developer activities.

From CKB Fundamentals to Practical Development

@longdevbf delivered the first community presentation, introducing CKB and helping the audience understand some of its core architecture, unique characteristics and the opportunities it offers developers.

@Tung_Pham followed with a broad explanation blockchain concepts before discussing CKB, quantum resistance and Quantum Purse. This provided useful context for attendees with different levels of familiarity with blockchain technology while also demonstrating how CKB’s flexibility translates to embracing quantum-resistant cryptography and a live, audited PQC wallet.

James then presented his hardware-related work involving the integration of Trezor hardware wallets with Quantum Purse. His session demonstrated how CKB’s cryptographic flexibility can be explored through practical development combining hardware and software.

Following James, @RetricSu from CKB DevRel provided an introduction to CKB development via a remote presentation. His session helped connect the earlier discussion about CKB with the practical foundations developers need to begin building.

Opportunities for Developers

As there was a substantial student contingent in the audience, my presentation focused on the importance of remaining open-minded as technology evolves. Students entering the industry today are likely to encounter technologies and applications that are still at an early stage (or may not yet exist at all), and blockchain is worth paying attention to as it continues to mature over the next decade. I also introduced the opportunities available through Nervos Community Catalyst, including CKBuilders, Build on CKB, hackathons and other contribution pathways within the CKB ecosystem.

Ngoc continued the programme by sharing his reflections on CKB and discussing his experience of building a ToyTrade marketplace. His presentation gave the audience insight into the development process from the perspective of someone actively learning about CKB and applying that knowledge to a working project.

@timnguyen concluded the presentations by discussing his experience of building CKB Lab and FiberGate, a project developed for the recent Fiber Network hackathon. His session showed how participation in CKBuilders and ecosystem hackathons can lead to the development of more substantial tools and projects over time.

A special note of thanks must be made to @zz_tovarishch who adapted his CKB mBabel tool to support en <> vn live on-screen translations during proceedings, as well as providing access to Volcengine services. This proved to be an invaluable resource for attendees, ensuring they were well-positioned to engage fully with the content delivered.

A Growing Builder Community in Vietnam

Across the programme, the speakers covered blockchain fundamentals, CKB development, post-quantum cryptography, hardware integration, application development and Fiber Network. This range reflected the different technical interests already developing within the Vietnamese CKBuilder community.

CKBuilder participants from Vietnam now numbers more than 15, with interest continuing to grow largely through personal recommendations and word of mouth. Although CKB community events have previously taken place in the country, CKB Off-Chain Hanoi was the first centred on CKBuilders and the first opportunity for many of them to meet and present their work in person. Their prominent role in the programme reflected the range of knowledge and projects already emerging from the Vietnamese community. Vietnam remains an important focal point because of its strong developer base, wider interest in blockchain and the experience many local developers already have with UTXO-based systems.

Reflections and Next Steps

CKB Off-Chain Hanoi was a strong first step for the CKBuilder community in Vietnam. It brought together developers, students and faculty members, created space for practical knowledge to be shared and gave local builders an opportunity to present their work.

We will continue exploring events and other activities in Vietnam, with a view to strengthening relationships between existing CKB builders while welcoming other regional developers who share our interests. The interest shown by the university faculty also creates opportunities for further engagement with students and other developers.

The aim is to build upon the connections established at this event and support a community in which local builders increasingly organise activities, exchange knowledge and help introduce other developers to CKB.
