item.title: Waymark — Recovering useful wallet state without starting from zero
item.dc:creator: Ticoworld
item.description:
Hi everyone,

I’ve been testing a recovery problem around CKB light-client wallets.

When you restore a wallet with your seed phrase, you get control of your wallet again.

But the wallet may still have to rebuild a lot of the local information it had already gathered before — account discovery, transaction history, live Cells, sync progress, light-client state, and other data it needs to become fully useful again.

I wanted to see if that part could also be recovered safely.

That became Waymark.

GitHub:

github.com

GitHub - Ticoworld/waymark

Contribute to Ticoworld/waymark development by creating an account on GitHub.

The idea

Waymark separates two things that normally get treated as one recovery problem:

1. Recovering ownership of the wallet

This still happens normally with the seed phrase.

The new installation creates its own keys, PIN protection, device security and signing environment.

2. Recovering useful local state

Before the old installation is lost, selected non-secret wallet and light-client state can be saved.

After the wallet is recovered normally on the new installation, that saved state can be restored too.

The wallet then continues syncing from there and checks everything against the chain.

So the flow looks like this:

Restore wallet normally
        ↓
keys and signing access are recovered
        ↓
restore saved non-secret wallet/light-client state
        ↓
continue syncing from that point
        ↓
catch up with anything that changed
        ↓
current chain state remains the final authority

The saved state is not treated as truth forever.

It can be old.

Cells that were live when it was saved may already have been spent. New transactions may have happened. Balances may have changed.

The wallet still has to reconnect to the chain and catch up correctly.

The point is simply that it does not always need to throw away all the useful work it had already done and start rebuilding everything from zero.

What is saved

The tested package contains selected non-secret information needed to continue the wallet’s previous work.

That includes things around:

  • public account relationships;
  • account and Script mapping;
  • sync progress;
  • discovery state;
  • light-client history and indexes;
  • chain checkpoints needed to continue syncing.

It does not contain the wallet’s signing secrets.

Waymark does not transfer:

  • seed phrase;
  • private keys;
  • wallet PIN;
  • Android device credential;
  • Android Keystore keys;
  • source-device signing material;
  • raw wallet backups containing secrets.

The wallet still has to be recovered normally first.

That was an important part of the test.

Why I tested it on Pocket Node

Pocket Node was a good place to test this because it runs a CKB light client directly on the device and keeps useful local state around the wallet.

I tested against Pocket Node 1.8.5.

Pocket itself was not modified into a finished Waymark feature.

The recovery/export/import work was done around the existing Pocket implementation so I could test whether the recovery model actually works.

How I tested it

I did not only test restoring a clean snapshot and checking whether the app opened.

The saved state was intentionally allowed to become stale.

After the checkpoint was created, more activity happened on the wallet.

That meant the restored wallet had to prove that it could continue from the older state and still discover what changed afterwards.

The later tests included:

  • two populated accounts;
  • different CKB Scripts;
  • transaction history on both accounts;
  • an active Nervos DAO deposit;
  • transactions that happened after the saved checkpoint;
  • account mapping checks;
  • balance and live Cell checks;
  • signing;
  • restart;
  • and comparison against the expected chain state.

After the emulator tests passed, I ran the full recovery flow on a real Android phone.

The final comparison

I tested two separate recovery paths.

Baseline recovery

For the baseline, Pocket started from fresh application state.

The wallet was recovered normally from the seed.

No saved Waymark state was used.

Pocket had to rebuild the required wallet/light-client state normally.

After recovery it reached the expected chain state, signed a real CKB testnet transaction, broadcast it successfully and passed a cold restart.

State-assisted recovery

Then Pocket was reset again.

The same wallet was recovered normally from the seed first.

This created fresh destination-side security again.

Only after normal recovery was complete did I restore the older saved non-secret state.

That saved checkpoint was stale by this point.

There had already been later activity on both accounts, including the transaction created during the baseline recovery.

So the restored wallet still had work to do.

It had to:

  • catch up from the saved checkpoint;
  • discover the later transactions;
  • remove Cells that were no longer live;
  • find the new live Cells;
  • recover the correct balances;
  • keep both accounts mapped correctly;
  • recover the DAO position correctly;
  • and reach the same current wallet state as the baseline recovery.

It passed.

After catching up, the state-assisted recovery also signed and confirmed another real testnet transaction.

It then passed a cold restart as well.

Result

At the common comparison point, baseline recovery and state-assisted recovery matched.

They agreed on:

  • both accounts;
  • account-to-Script mapping;
  • live Cells;
  • balances;
  • covered transaction history;
  • later activity that happened after the saved checkpoint;
  • DAO ownership and deposit state;
  • and sync progress.

There was no recovery-specific DAO difference.

There was no account mix-up.

There was no dependency on the old device’s Keystore.

The destination created its own fresh security state and signing still worked after the saved state was restored.

So for the Pocket setup I tested, the result was:

PASS

The baseline test transaction was:

0x2067edf16ab143e7bff9ef91803e36ce6a32347c632c75a37d382443ae379738

The state-assisted test transaction was:

0xe4cbdffa9002b0283c2c71cc19ec646b85cb58274b8f45d72496e78ae96b4cbd

Both were confirmed on CKB testnet.

More detailed evidence is in the repository:

github.com

GitHub - Ticoworld/waymark

Contribute to Ticoworld/waymark development by creating an account on GitHub.

What about recovery time?

On the real-phone run, the full baseline path took about 60 minutes.

The state-assisted path took about 30 minutes.

But I do not want to present that as “Waymark is 2x faster.”

These were not controlled performance benchmarks.

The runs included things like:

  • manual authentication;
  • automation delays;
  • peer/network conditions;
  • discovery work;
  • observation and verification;
  • restart checks.

The useful result is simpler:

the restored state avoided rebuilding some work, and the wallet still reached the same correct chain state.

A proper performance benchmark would need a different test setup.

Why I think this matters

Wallet recovery is usually discussed mostly as:

Can I recover my keys?

That is obviously the most important part.

But with a light-client wallet, there is another question:

Can I also recover the useful work my wallet had already done?

Those are different things.

The seed answers:

“Which wallet do I own?”

The saved state can help answer:

“What had this wallet already discovered and processed?”

Waymark keeps those responsibilities separate.

The seed and keys remain responsible for ownership and signing.

The saved state only helps the recovered wallet continue from previous work.

And the chain remains responsible for telling the wallet what is currently true.

One useful thing I found while testing

While checking the DAO state during this work, I also found a separate issue in Pocket’s DAO reward estimate.

The DAO reader was using 61 CKB as the occupied capacity when calculating compensation, while a DAO deposit Cell actually occupies 102 CKB.

That caused the displayed compensation estimate to be slightly too high.

It did not affect wallet ownership, principal or the actual unlock transaction path.

I reported it here:

github.com/RaheemJnr/pocket-node

fix(dao): DaoDepositReader still uses 61 CKB occupied capacity for compensation

opened 12:37PM - 06 Oct 26 UTC
closed 05:46PM - 06 Oct 26 UTC
Ticoworld

## Summary While testing a real 1,000 CKB DAO deposit on Pocket v1.8.5, I found… that `DaoDepositReader` still calculates DAO compensation using 61 CKB occupied capacity instead of 102 CKB. This appears to be a remaining reader/display issue related to the older fix in #315. The actual unlock path now uses the correct 102 CKB value, but the DAO reader still passes `61_00000000L` when calculating displayed compensation. ## Observed Testnet DAO deposit: - Principal: 1,000 CKB - Pocket cached compensation: 22,530 shannons - Canonical compensation at the same comparison point: 21,546 shannons Pocket's value is slightly higher than the canonical result. ## Root cause A standard DAO deposit Cell occupies: - 8 bytes capacity - 53 bytes lock Script - 33 bytes DAO type Script - 8 bytes data Total: 102 bytes / 102 CKB occupied capacity. Pocket already defines the correct value as: `DaoConstants.DEPOSIT_OCCUPIED_SHANNONS = 10_200_000_000L` However, `DaoDepositReader.kt` still passes: `61_00000000L` to `nativeCalculateMaxWithdraw()` in both: - active deposited-cell compensation calculation - withdrawing-cell compensation calculation This effectively treats an extra 41 CKB as compensation-bearing capacity and slightly inflates the displayed reward. ## Relation to #315 #315 previously fixed the same 61 vs 102 CKB occupied-capacity issue in the actual phase-2 unlock path. That path now uses the correct 102 CKB constant. This issue is for the remaining calculation in `DaoDepositReader`. ## Impact From the paths checked: - DAO ownership/state identity is unaffected - deposit principal is unaffected - actual unlock calculation uses the correct 102 CKB value - displayed/cached compensation is slightly too high - derived totals/APC may also be affected ## Suggested fix Replace the hardcoded `61_00000000L` values in `DaoDepositReader` with: `DaoConstants.DEPOSIT_OCCUPIED_SHANNONS` in both compensation branches. ## Acceptance - Active DAO deposit compensation matches the canonical calculation - Withdrawing DAO compensation uses 102 CKB occupied capacity - Existing unlock behavior remains unchanged

The fix was added, tested and merged into Pocket:

github.com/RaheemJnr/pocket-node

fix(dao): compensation uses the 102 CKB a deposit cell occupies, not 61 (#550) (#551)

main ← fix/550-dao-occupied-capacity
opened 05:31PM - 06 Oct 26 UTC
RaheemJnr
+419 -17

## Problem `DaoDepositReader` passed `61_00000000L` (61 CKB, the size of a plai…n secp256k1 cell) as the occupied capacity to `nativeCalculateMaxWithdraw`, for both deposited and withdrawing cells. A Nervos DAO deposit cell occupies 102 CKB (8 capacity + 53 lock + 33 type + 8 data), and the occupied part earns no compensation. The unlock transaction already used `DaoConstants.DEPOSIT_OCCUPIED_SHANNONS` (102 CKB), so only the displayed and cached compensation was wrong. Effect: every displayed compensation was inflated by `(C - 61) / (C - 102)`. The reporter's 1,000 CKB deposit showed 22,530 shannons against the canonical 21,546, which is exactly `21,546 * 939 / 898`. Principal, ownership and the unlock transaction were never affected. ## What changed - `DaoDepositReader`: both branches now go through one private `compensationFor(depositDao, endDao, capacity)` helper that passes `DaoConstants.DEPOSIT_OCCUPIED_SHANNONS`. No other place in app, shared, iOS Swift or the Rust bridge computes DAO compensation with a hardcoded occupied value (the Rust `calculate_max_withdraw` takes it as a parameter; the iOS app does not call it yet). The 61 CKB values in `SendViewModel` and `TransactionBuilder.MIN_CELL_CAPACITY` are the correct minimum secp256k1 cell size and are untouched. - Cache: live DAO cells are recomputed on every scan and written through to `dao_cells`, so they correct themselves on the next refresh. A row the live scan no longer returns (outside the sync window, or mid-unlock) was shown from its stored `compensation` and never rewritten, so a withdrawing position there would have kept the inflated figure for good. `GatewayRepository.mergeWithCachedDaoDeposits` now recomputes those rows via `DaoDepositReader.recomputeCachedCompensation`, using only the Room header cache (never waits on peers): a withdrawing row is measured to its withdraw block, a deposited row to the current tip. The corrected value is written back when it changed, through a new `DaoCellDao.updateCompensation` that sets only the `compensation` column and skips a `COMPLETED` row (matched on txHash, index, network and walletId). A whole-row upsert of the copy read earlier in the merge would race #529's retirement and bring a claimed deposit back. If a header is not cached, the stored row is shown as before. No Room migration, no schema change. - Totals: total compensation, per-deposit APC and the weighted APC in the overview and DAO screen all derive from `DaoDeposit.compensation`, so they follow without a separate change. ## Tests - New `DaoDepositReaderCompensationTest` (6 tests): the occupied capacity passed for a deposited cell and for a withdrawing cell is `DEPOSIT_OCCUPIED_SHANNONS`; cached withdrawing and deposited rows are recomputed against the right end block; a missing header or a withdrawing row without a withdraw header leaves the stored value alone. - It reuses `DaoUnlockShadowLightClientNative` (extended with `nativeGetCells`, a recorded call list for max-withdraw, and an optional transaction override) instead of a second shadow, since `LightClientNative` is a Kotlin object and Robolectric binds one shadow per sandbox. - Two new `GatewayRepositoryDaoUnlockTest` cases. In the first, a cached mid-unlock row is retired `COMPLETED` while its compensation is being recomputed, and it must stay `COMPLETED`. In the second, an outside-window row's recomputed compensation is shown and written back without changing its status. - Mutation probes: putting `61_00000000L` back makes the 4 compensation tests fail (`occupied=6100000000` vs expected `10200000000`). Putting back the whole-row `upsertDaoCell(entity.copy(...))` makes the retirement test fail (`expected:<[COMPLETED]> but was:<[UNLOCKABLE]>`). - `./gradlew test :shared:testAndroidHostTest :app:assembleDebug :app:checkNoCkbSdkOnRuntimeClasspath -x cargoBuild`: green. App unit tests go from 1113 to 1121 per variant; shared stays at 263. Fixes #550 Thanks @Ticoworld for the precise report.

That issue was separate from the Waymark recovery result, but it came out of the testing.

Current scope

Waymark is not a finished production wallet feature.

It is also not something I am claiming already works across every CKB wallet.

The current end-to-end proof is on Pocket Node.

I have not yet validated the same recovery flow on:

  • Neuron;
  • iBytes;
  • or other CKB wallets/light-client applications.

The current proof is also limited to the environment I tested:

  • one pinned Pocket version;
  • CKB testnet;
  • two accounts;
  • one active DAO deposit;
  • one real Android device;
  • and the specific saved-state format used in the experiment.

Things like cross-version migration, different wallet architectures, much larger histories, hostile/corrupt source backups and production backup UX still need separate work if this goes further.

What happens next?

For now I wanted to put the result in front of the CKB community rather than keep testing more wallets privately.

The main question I have is:

Is this recovery model useful enough to explore beyond Pocket?

For example:

  • Should something like this simply become a Pocket feature?
  • Would it be useful to test the same recovery model on another CKB wallet or light-client application?
  • If the same need appears in multiple wallets, is there a useful reusable part?
  • Or is wallet state recovery something each wallet should own independently?

I think the Pocket proof is enough to have that discussion now.

If there is interest, the next step can be decided from there instead of trying to build support for every wallet first.

GitHub - Ticoworld/waymark

Contribute to Ticoworld/waymark development by creating an account on GitHub.

Feedback from wallet developers, light-client developers and anyone who has dealt with wallet recovery/state reconstruction would be very useful.

item.title: Towards a Based EVM Layer on CKB: Three Architectural Options
item.dc:creator: ArthurZhang
item.description:
Option 1: A Based ZK Rollup on CKB

When discussing an EVM environment on CKB, the conversation usually begins with execution: Solidity compatibility, Ethereum RPCs and the migration of existing DeFi protocols.

Yet execution may no longer be the defining question. Mature EVM implementations already exist. The harder questions concern who orders the next batch, what CKB itself ought to verify, and how users retain control over their assets when execution takes place elsewhere.

I have been exploring whether Myelin could provide the off-chain foundation for a based EVM architecture whose canonical ordering and settlement are governed by CKB itself.

I see three possible architectures worth exploring:

  • Option 1 — Based ZK Rollup: CKB provides canonical sequencing, L1 data availability and validity-proof settlement.

  • Option 2 — Based ZK Validium: The same sequencing and validity-proof model, but with external data availability to support higher throughput.

  • Option 3 — Based Optimistic Rollup: CKB provides canonical sequencing and data availability, while disputed EVM execution is adjudicated through a CKB-VM-compatible court rather than continuous ZK proving.

These options explore two distinct design choices: where transaction data resides, and how execution correctness is established. All three retain CKB as the canonical sequencing and settlement authority, while Myelin provides the off-chain execution and evidence infrastructure.

Option 3 is particularly interesting in relation to Myelin’s original CKB-isomorphic execution model, although extending its existing court machinery to EVM semantics would require substantial additional work.

This first post focuses on Option 1, with the other two explored separately in the thread.

The idea follows my earlier discussion, Introducing Myelin: a CKB-aligned off-chain Cell session runtime.

Myelin began as an experiment in preserving CKB transaction semantics across off-chain sessions: deterministic execution, dependency scheduling, persistent state, evidence commitments and a path towards L1 adjudication. It was deliberately not presented as a new permissionless chain.

An EVM Rollup would require a separate execution backend, but much of Myelin’s surrounding runtime machinery could be useful. More importantly, it raises an architectural possibility worth examining: using CKB’s own consensus and Cell model to establish the canonical history of an EVM ledger, without appointing a permanent L2 sequencer.

This is a design proposal, not an announcement of an implemented Rollup.

What makes a Rollup based?

The term comes from Justin Drake’s original proposal.

In a conventional Rollup, an L2 sequencer typically collects transactions, chooses their order and submits batches to L1. Even where users have a forced-inclusion mechanism, the sequencer retains considerable influence over transaction ordering and short-term censorship.

A based Rollup takes a different approach. The underlying L1 determines the canonical sequence of L2 blocks. The right to propose the next Rollup block is permissionless, rather than reserved for an appointed L2 operator.

The important distinction is not whether an L2 block eventually appears on L1. Almost every Rollup does that. It is whether a privileged actor controls which L2 blocks may advance the chain.

For CKB, this would mean allowing competing builders to assemble EVM batches, while CKB miners determine their canonical inclusion through ordinary PoW consensus.

There would be no separate L2 committee whose signatures establish the authoritative batch sequence.

This does not eliminate MEV or guarantee immediate confirmations. Builders still influence transaction ordering within their batches, and ordering competition moves towards the L1 block-building and fee market. CKB also has its own transaction proposal window, so the latency and preconfirmation model would differ from Ethereum-based designs.

Nevertheless, the attraction is considerable: the Rollup need not maintain a second political or economic authority over its canonical history.

Why the Cell model is particularly interesting

CKB has a useful property which is easy to overlook in discussions dominated by account-based contracts.

A Cell can only be consumed once in the canonical chain.

Suppose a Rollup maintains a SequencingTip Cell representing its current ordered batch frontier. A valid proposal consumes that Cell and creates a successor with the next batch commitment.

Two competing proposals cannot both become successors of the same Cell in the same canonical history.

This gives us a native, L1-enforced linearisation point.

flowchart TB
    A["Permissionless EVM batch builders"] --> B1["Candidate batch A"]
    A --> B2["Candidate batch B"]

    S["Current SequencingTip Cell"]

    S --> B1
    S --> B2

    B1 --> C{"CKB canonical inclusion"}
    B2 --> C

    C --> D["One accepted successor"]
    C -.-> R["Conflicting spend cannot survive"]

    D --> E["Next SequencingTip Cell"]
    E --> F["Canonical EVM batch stream"]

    classDef builder fill:#edf3ff,stroke:#6487ca,color:#1f3c75
    classDef canonical fill:#daf3e7,stroke:#38936d,color:#14573e
    classDef reject fill:#fff0eb,stroke:#cb806e,color:#8b4031

    class A,B1,B2 builder
    class S,C,D,E,F canonical
    class R reject

The Type Script would enforce the transition rules: the previous tip must be consumed, the successor must preserve the Rollup identity, and the new batch commitment must be correctly formed and linked to the old one. Crucially, advancing this Cell would not require a designated sequencer’s signature.

This is not a free scaling solution. A singleton sequencing Cell creates contention, and CKB’s proposal/commit mechanism complicates successive batch production.

My preferred starting point is to separate parallel transaction intake from L1 canonicalisation. Myelin could execute bounded microbatches off-chain, which are then assembled into ordered epoch manifests, with one CKB sequencing transition per epoch.

This amortises contention rather than eliminating it. The sustainable checkpoint rate would still need to be measured under realistic CKB transaction-dependency conditions.

There is another important requirement: users must be able to submit transactions without depending on a particular builder.

I would distinguish ordinary batch-data publication from a separate, authenticated priority inbox on CKB.

The first provides the transaction data needed for independent reconstruction. The second provides a potential route for forced inclusion when ordinary builders refuse to process a user’s transaction.

The priority inbox would need explicit admission rules, resource limits, deterministic rejection semantics and verifiable processing obligations. Simply recording requests on L1 would not, by itself, guarantee their execution.

Its ordering and completeness must also be authenticated without trusting an off-chain indexer’s interpretation of CKB history.

These are protocol responsibilities, rather than details that can safely be delegated to the mempool.

Myelin as an execution and evidence substrate

I would separate the system into three responsibilities:

  • CKB determines the canonical order of accepted batches, authenticates the sequencing history and enforces verified settlement.
  • Myelin reconstructs that history, executes the corresponding state transitions and provides the infrastructure for independent state reconstruction.
  • Independent provers demonstrate that the EVM state transitions conform to the committed execution rules.

The proposed architecture would look roughly as follows:

flowchart TB
    subgraph USER["Ethereum application surface"]
        U["Wallets and Solidity applications"]
        B["Permissionless batch builders"]
        U --> B
    end

    subgraph CKB["CKB Layer 1 · PoW authority"]
        D["L1 batch-data publication"]
        I["Authenticated priority inbox"]
        O["SequencingTip Cell<br/>Canonical ordering frontier"]
        S["SettlementTip Cell<br/>Verified EVM state"]
        V["Asset vaults and withdrawal claims"]

        D --> O
        I -.-> O
        S --> V
    end

    subgraph MYELIN["Myelin · Off-chain runtime"]
        F["Canonical CKB follower"]
        E["EVM execution and state reconstruction"]
        P["Independent validity prover"]

        F --> E --> P
    end

    B --> D
    U -. "Forced inclusion" .-> I
    O --> F
    D -. "Published execution data" .-> F
    O -. "Authenticated history" .-> S
    P --> S
    V -. "Deposits and exits" .-> E

    style USER fill:#f4f0ff,stroke:#9b87c6,stroke-width:2px
    style CKB fill:#eaf3ff,stroke:#6b91c9,stroke-width:2px
    style MYELIN fill:#e9f6f0,stroke:#6fae91,stroke-width:2px

The proposed EVM execution profile would use an established Ethereum execution engine, such as revm, with canonical Ethereum account and storage semantics.

This deserves a distinction from Myelin’s original design.

The existing Cell execution model is CKB-isomorphic: its transactions and scripts are deliberately shaped to remain compatible with CKB-VM. EVM execution cannot simply inherit that claim. Ethereum has a different state model, execution semantics and gas accounting.

I would therefore retain native Cell sessions as one Myelin execution profile and introduce EVM execution as another.

They could share infrastructure for deterministic batch processing, recovery, durable state lineage and evidence generation, without pretending their virtual machines are equivalent.

For the EVM profile, correctness would be established through validity proofs rather than direct CKB-VM replay of every EVM instruction.

CKB would verify the proof, not emulate Ethereum.

There is also an unresolved data-publication question within the Rollup design itself.

CKB transaction witnesses, Cell data and other CKB-committed data structures have different storage, retrieval and economic properties. The precise data carrier must ensure that independent participants can retrieve the ordered transaction inputs needed for state reconstruction.

Merely committing to a data hash is not sufficient for Rollup-grade data availability.

Two frontiers instead of a second consensus network

The part of this design I find most promising is to separate the ordering frontier from the proven-state frontier.

The first advances when CKB accepts the next canonical batch. The second advances when a validity proof establishes the resulting EVM state transition.

They need not advance at the same pace.

flowchart TB
    subgraph ORDER["CKB ordering frontier"]
        direction LR
        O0["Order 0"] -->|"Batch A"| O1["Order 1"]
        O1 -->|"Batch B"| O2["Order 2"]
        O2 -->|"Batch C"| O3["Order 3"]
    end

    subgraph PROOF["Verified settlement frontier"]
        direction LR
        P0["State 0"] -->|"Proof A"| P1["State 1"]
        P1 -->|"Aggregated proof B + C"| P3["State 3"]
    end

    O1 -. "Verified ordered prefix" .-> P1
    O3 -. "Verified ordered prefix" .-> P3

    classDef ordered fill:#dfeaff,stroke:#668bd1,color:#203e77
    classDef proven fill:#ddf3e5,stroke:#55a37b,color:#195c3d

    class O0,O1,O2,O3 ordered
    class P0,P1,P3 proven

    style ORDER fill:#f5f8ff,stroke:#a6bce5
    style PROOF fill:#f1fbf5,stroke:#9ed0b3

The ordering commitment would bind each new batch to the previous commitment. Separately, the settlement Cell would hold the latest verified Ethereum state root and the highest proven batch index.

A proof authorising settlement must establish that it has executed the next contiguous range of the canonical CKB-ordered batch history, starting from the previously verified state.

The verifier’s public inputs would bind the Rollup identity, protocol version, execution rules, authenticated batch range, previous state root, new state root and withdrawal commitment.

One detail that deserves particular attention is how the settlement verifier authenticates that historical batch range.

A simple hash chain establishes succession, but does not necessarily provide efficient proofs that an older range belongs to the accepted history.

An append-only authenticated accumulator, CKB-authorised batch receipts, or an equivalent mechanism supporting verifiable prefix extensions may therefore be needed.

The settlement script must verify the relationship against authenticated CKB sequencing state, rather than accepting a prover-supplied account of canonical history. The precise commitment structure and its CKB-VM verification cost remain to be specified.

This separation would let different parties participate without granting any of them permanent authority over the ledger.

A miner or builder could propose a batch without producing its validity proof. A prover could settle a range of batches without deciding their order. A full node could independently reconstruct the EVM state from published transaction data.

There is, however, an important liveness problem.

An unproven batch must not become an irreversible obstruction merely because its builder supplied malformed data or an impossible execution workload.

The batch format, admission rules, resource bounds and treatment of rejected transactions must make every admissible ordered entry deterministically processable.

Otherwise, separating ordering from proving would introduce a denial-of-service mechanism.

The settlement logic must also account for prover disappearance. Permissionless proof generation removes dependence on a particular prover in principle; practical recovery additionally requires public data, reproducible proving inputs and a workable exit path.

These are the areas where I would concentrate much of the protocol design.

How this differs from Godwoken

It would be misleading to discuss an EVM Rollup on CKB without acknowledging Godwoken.

Godwoken and Polyjuice established that an EVM-compatible execution environment could be built above CKB.

The original Godwoken framework was intended to support permissionless Rollup configurations, while its early deployments used an optimistic-Rollup design and PoA-controlled L2 block issuance.

That work addressed a genuine limitation in the ecosystem: Ethereum developers could not otherwise bring their existing contracts and tooling into a scalable CKB-connected environment so readily.

I regard the proposed based design as a continuation of that research direction, with a different emphasis.

Dimension Early Godwoken architecture Proposed Myelin-based ZK Rollup
Execution Polyjuice EVM Ethereum-equivalent execution backend
Block ordering PoA-controlled L2 production in early deployments Permissionless batch proposals, canonical sequence determined by CKB
State verification Optimistic/challenge-oriented design Validity-proof-oriented settlement
L1 responsibility Rollup commitments, contracts and settlement Canonical ordering, L1 data publication, proof verification and settlement
Off-chain infrastructure Godwoken-specific Rollup node Myelin runtime extended with an EVM profile

These are comparisons of architectural models, not a claim that Godwoken never contemplated other consensus mechanisms or ZK configurations.

The distinction I care about is where authority resides.

Godwoken’s early architecture provided an Ethereum-like execution environment whose blocks were produced by an L2 authority set and committed to CKB.

In a genuinely based design, L1 consensus determines which permissionlessly proposed Rollup batches become canonical. The proof system determines whether the resulting state can be settled.

This is not the same as guaranteeing transaction-level fairness.

Builders would still choose the order of ordinary transactions within their batches, subject to whatever inclusion and ordering constraints the protocol enforces.

Meaningful censorship resistance would therefore require an authenticated forced-inclusion path, rather than relying on permissionless batch publication alone.

There is a difference between using CKB as a place to publish Rollup commitments and allowing its consensus to govern the canonical extension of the Rollup’s execution history.

That latter possibility seems underexplored.

What kind of ecosystem could emerge?

The immediate attraction is familiar: Solidity contracts, Ethereum wallets, automated market makers, lending protocols, stablecoins and the wider body of EVM tooling.

But simply creating another EVM environment with a bridge to CKB would offer a rather limited proposition.

The more interesting opportunity is to combine Ethereum’s composable execution environment with CKB-native ownership and settlement semantics.

Consider CKB-native assets such as xUDT tokens. Their custody and issuance constraints could remain enforced through CKB Cells, while representations of those assets circulate in an EVM environment offering AMMs, lending markets and other financial primitives.

An asset might originate under a CellScript-defined issuance or redemption policy on L1 and gain access to EVM liquidity through a proof-secured vault.

Returns to L1 would be authorised against verified withdrawal commitments rather than an operator’s discretionary approval.

The two environments would retain different strengths. EVM provides a familiar programmable financial environment; CKB retains the underlying asset custody rules.

Cross-layer interactions would still be asynchronous, and their bridge contracts would form a significant security boundary. This proposal should not be mistaken for atomic EVM–CKB composability.

The availability of liquid stablecoins would be particularly important.

Deep markets cannot be obtained from execution compatibility alone. A technically correct AMM without useful collateral, stablecoin liquidity or reliable price discovery is not much of a financial system.

Another possibility concerns Fiber.

A mature Fiber ecosystem could provide payment and liquidity-routing services around the Rollup, whilst the EVM environment handles more complex programmable positions and CKB provides asset settlement.

The integration would need explicit message and trust boundaries, but the complementary roles are worth exploring.

There may also be room for RFQ markets, tokenised real-world asset workflows and agent-operated financial applications, especially where the origin of an asset, the rules governing its custody and its trading environment ought to remain separately verifiable.

I find the economic implications interesting as well.

If applications depend on CKB for canonical ordering, batch publication and proof-backed settlement, their activity creates demand for CKB block space.

That is a different relationship from an L2 which merely posts an occasional state commitment whilst most of its economic activity remains within a proprietary ordering system.

It would connect a portion of Rollup activity to the existing L1 fee market.

Of course, the economic significance would depend on actual usage, fee levels and the resulting demand for block space. More L2 transactions do not automatically translate into proportionally greater L1 revenue.

There is also a hard capacity constraint.

CKB’s block space is finite, and publishing complete Rollup transaction data is more expensive than publishing a commitment alone.

A validity proof solves execution verification; it does not solve data availability.

For a trust-minimised Rollup, independent parties must be able to reconstruct the state from available batch data.

Using external DA instead would create a different security model, closer to a Validium. That is the motivation for the second architectural option discussed separately in this thread.

Any claim of economically viable throughput needs to be tested against CKB’s actual data capacity, transaction costs, canonicalisation rate and proof-verification budget.

Why I think this is worth exploring

The idea appeals to me partly because it does not require CKB to imitate Ethereum.

CKB would continue to do what its architecture is particularly well suited to: enforce precise state-transition constraints, establish ownership through live Cells, provide a common consensus history and verify programmes or proofs under CKB-VM.

The EVM can remain the EVM, with its own account state, execution rules and developer ecosystem.

Myelin would provide the off-chain machinery connecting those worlds, with strict boundaries between CKB-native execution, EVM execution and the evidence accepted at settlement.

There are plenty of unresolved questions.

A contested singleton sequencing Cell may be a poor throughput primitive under realistic CKB transaction-proposal conditions. An authenticated forced-inclusion queue is considerably harder to design than an ordinary off-chain mempool.

Efficient verification of historical batch prefixes also needs careful work. Proof verification costs, L1 data economics, bridge safety, prover liveness and emergency exits all deserve serious scrutiny.

I would be interested in challenges to these assumptions, especially from people familiar with CKB consensus, transaction dependencies and script verification.

The ambition is not to recreate Godwoken under a different name.

It is to investigate whether CKB’s PoW consensus and Cell model can provide canonical ordering for permissionlessly proposed EVM batches, without introducing a privileged L2 sequencing authority.

Transaction ordering within those batches would still require explicit rules, particularly around forced inclusion and censorship resistance.

The underlying research question is whether CKB can enforce a uniquely ordered, permissionlessly extensible and efficiently verifiable execution history, while allowing settlement to advance independently of sequencing.

If that can be established, the next question is how best to secure execution and data availability: through validity proofs or optimistic adjudication, with data published on CKB or an external network. The three options discussed here explore different trade-offs within that design space.

That seems a worthwhile direction for Myelin to explore.

  • Myelin repository
  • Based rollups — superpowers from L1 sequencing, Justin Drake
  • Towards CKB-style Lego pieces: Polyjuice on Godwoken

item.title: Introducing CKAutomata: Payment Automation and Nervos DAO Harvest on CKB
item.dc:creator: Hallab
item.description:
Hello everyone,

I have been working on CKAutomata, a payment automation application built for CKB.

The idea is simple: you choose what a payment should do and when it should happen. Your wallet
shows you the complete plan before you approve it. CKAutomata then watches the chain and submits
only the payment you approved when the right time arrives.

The main feature is Nervos DAO Harvest. It helps a user collect earned DAO compensation and put
the original CKB amount back into a new DAO deposit without having to remember each withdrawal
step. CKAutomata also supports one-time scheduled payments and recurring payments.

CKAutomata is live on CKB Testnet. It does not hold a user’s private key, and the service cannot
change the approved amount, recipient, schedule, or recovery address.

Project Links

  • Try CKAutomata
  • Repository
  • Read on How it works guide
  • View testnet automations

The Problem: Some Payments Still Need You to Come Back Later

Many CKB actions cannot be completed in one sitting.

A Nervos DAO user may need to wait for the right withdrawal window, prepare the withdrawal, wait
again for it to mature, claim the CKB, separate the earned compensation, and make a new deposit.
Missing the right time can mean waiting for another DAO cycle.

The same problem appears in normal payments. A user may want to send CKB next week or pay the same
recipient every month. Today, the user or an application server must remember the date and submit
each transaction.

CKB can check whether a payment follows the rules, but the chain does not wake up and send a
transaction by itself. CKAutomata adds that missing payment service. It watches for the right time,
builds the approved transaction, and submits it for CKB to check.

Main Feature: Nervos DAO Harvest

Nervos DAO lets CKB holders earn compensation while their CKB is deposited. Withdrawing from the
DAO is a two-step process.

First, the deposit must be prepared for withdrawal. After that, the user must wait until the
withdrawal becomes mature before the CKB can be claimed. This process is described in
RFC 23.

Harvest Compensation automates this cycle for users who want to receive the earned compensation
while keeping the original amount in Nervos DAO.

How the Harvest Works

  1. Choose the original amount. The user chooses the amount of CKB that should remain in Nervos
    DAO.
  2. Choose the compensation address. This is where the earned compensation will be sent after
    each completed harvest.
  3. Choose how many harvests to run. The user can choose one harvest or a fixed number of
    harvests. CKAutomata cannot add more later.
  4. Review the full deposit. The review shows the original amount, the automation charges, and
    the total amount the wallet will deposit. The charges are added separately and do not reduce the
    chosen original amount. Part of the extra amount is a reserve needed by the on-chain
    automation.
  5. Approve once. The wallet signs the setup transaction and locks in the exact amount,
    compensation address, number of harvests, charges, and recovery rules.
  6. Wait for the right DAO window. CKAutomata tracks the DAO cycle and prepares the withdrawal
    when the approved rules allow it.
  7. Wait for maturity. Nervos DAO still requires the normal waiting period. CKAutomata cannot
    skip or shorten it.
  8. Collect and deposit again. After maturity, the earned compensation goes to the chosen
    address and the exact original amount enters a new DAO deposit.
  9. Repeat only when approved. If the user selected more harvests, the next cycle begins. After
    the final harvest, no new cycle is created.

For example, if a user chooses 10,000 CKB as the original amount, that exact 10,000 CKB is the
amount that must return to Nervos DAO after each harvest. Only the compensation earned above that
amount is sent to the compensation address.

Who Controls the DAO Funds?

The user’s wallet approves the rules at the beginning. CKAutomata’s contracts then limit what an
executor can do with the deposited funds.

The owner keeps separate wallet-controlled options:

  • Stop prevents another harvest cycle from being created.
  • Exit begins the normal DAO withdrawal process so the owner can leave the automation.
  • Recover returns mature funds through the owner’s approved recovery path if the service is
    unavailable or the automation cannot continue.

If a DAO withdrawal has already been prepared but is not mature, The owner must wait for the normal maturity time before recovery can finish.

Other Payment Automation

Scheduled Payment

A user chooses an amount, recipient, refund address, and future date and time. The payment cannot be completed before that time. When the time arrives, CKAutomata submits the
approved recipient. The user can cancel or recover a live payment with the owner
wallet.

Recurring Payments

A user chooses one recipient, one amount for every payment, the first payment date, how often the
payment should repeat, and the total number of payments.

After each payment, the contracts create one next payment with the same recipient and amount. The
executor cannot add more payments or change the schedule. After the final payment, the automation
ends and the remaining value follows the approved owner return.

Recurring payments are fully funded when they are created. They are not an unlimited permission
to take money from the user’s wallet later.

Why CKB Is a Good Fit

On CKB, an automation can live in its own cell. That cell can record the payment rules, schedule,
remaining amount, executor charge, and owner recovery details.

CKB’s since rule
can stop a payment from being accepted too early. The CKAutomata scripts also check the payment
recipient, amount, executor reward, remaining funds, and next payment together.

This means the executor provides the action, but CKB provides the final check.

The wallet connection uses CCC. CCC completes the wallet
inputs, network fee, change, signing, and submission. CKAutomata checks the completed transaction
again before asking the user to approve it.

How Automatic Payments Are Completed

The current payment flow has five simple parts:

  1. The user chooses DAO Harvest, Scheduled Payment, or Recurring Payments.
  2. CKAutomata shows the complete amount, charges, destination, timing, and recovery rules.
  3. The user’s wallet approves the exact setup transaction.
  4. CKAutomata watches the chain and submits the approved payment when it becomes ready.
  5. CKB scripts check the transaction. A correct transaction completes; an incorrect one is
    rejected.

What Works Today

The current CKB Testnet release includes:

  • Nervos DAO Harvest setup, cycle tracking, compensation payment, repeat deposit, stop, exit, and
    recovery tools.
  • One-time scheduled CKB payments.
  • Finite recurring CKB payments.
  • Wallet connection, transaction review, signing, and submission through CCC.
  • Deployed CKB contracts for payment rules, DAO funds, automation jobs, and owner recovery.
  • Two live executors supporting Harvest, scheduled, and recurring payments.
  • A public automation dashboard, activity history, confirmation progress, and transaction links.
  • Tests for contracts, payment building, failures, recovery, APIs, executors, and browser flows.

The blockchain remains the final record. The dashboard and database help people read what is
happening, but they cannot change the on-chain payment rules.

Try CKAutomata

Open the live application and connect a supported wallet on CKB
Testnet.

Start with Harvest Compensation to review the original DAO amount, compensation address,
number of harvests, charges, and owner recovery controls. You can also create a Scheduled Payment
or Recurring Payments plan.

After submission, open Automations to follow it through confirmation, waiting, processing, and
completion. The How it works page explains every
flow without requiring knowledge of block numbers or transaction details.

Use only testnet funds and review every wallet request. The current deployment is an open testnet
experiment, not a production financial service.

What Comes Next

The next work is focused on making Harvest Compensation safer and reliable
over many DAO cycles. This includes more testnet use, clear measurement of charges and timing.

CKAutomata will also continue improving scheduled and recurring payments and make it easier for
other CKB applications to add payment automation without building their own private-key bot.

Feedback From the Community

I would especially appreciate feedback on:

  • Whether Harvest Compensation would be useful to Nervos DAO users.
  • Whether the Harvest steps, charges, waiting time, and recovery choices are easy to understand.
  • Which part of the Harvest contracts should receive the deepest independent review.
  • Which scheduled or recurring CKB payments people currently handle manually.
  • Which part of the CKAutomata need changes, fix or improvement.

Thanks for reading. I look forward to discussing the design and improving CKAutomata in the open.

item.title: [DIS] Kirea Finance: Native RWA Lending Infrastructure for CKB |【DIS】Kirea Finance：面向 CKB 的原生 RWA 借贷基础设施
item.dc:creator: SalmanDev
item.description:
Summary

Kirea Finance is open-source infrastructure for compliant, native real-world asset (RWA) claims on CKB: a unique-asset pattern, an issuer-revocable KYC attestation cell, and a fixed-term lending contract that uses both. The full flow is implemented and verified end to end on the CKB testnet, with no bridge or custodian required. By open-sourcing these reusable primitives for RWA collateral, issuer-controlled KYC, and fixed-term lending, this work expands the native DeFi capabilities available to CKB projects without relying on bridges or custodians.

This proposal requests $7,250 to harden that infrastructure so other CKB projects can build on it: strengthening the lending contract’s security by enforcing loan rules on every collateral spend and verifying net disbursement and repayment, integrating a live KYC provider, and handling repayment edge cases.

Grant Amount Requested: $7,250
ETA to Completion: 10 weeks from approval
CKB Wallet: ckb1qyqvaj4pmuw9vxurdlg8lx3sv7ywmcge33vsvrvu39
Repository: GitHub - salmansarwarr/Kirea-finance: RWA and lending prototype on CKB with no bridge, no custodian · GitHub

Problem

Tokenizing real-world assets is becoming a major cornerstone for the blockchain industry, yet CKB currently lacks an established pattern for lending against real-world asset claims in a compliant way. While CKB possesses robust DeFi infrastructure, the ecosystem remains constrained by limited access to real-world asset ownership and yields.

An earlier, larger attempt at RWA on CKB aimed to build a full platform, combining a custom identity system, reputation engine, and complete dynamic lending engine in one pass. That scope proved too broad for the team to complete alongside other priorities.

This proposal deliberately takes a narrower slice to solve the core problem: one real asset type (invoice), an established KYC vendor integration (Sumsub), and one simple fixed-term loan mechanic rather than a dynamic collateral-ratio engine. The aim is to harden and generalize the underlying pattern for easily onboarding future assets, not to replicate the full scope of that earlier attempt.

What’s Already Implemented

  • Native Asset Claims: RWA claims are issued natively on CKB as unique cells using the Type-ID pattern (no bridge required).
  • On-Chain Attestation: An issuer-revocable KYC attestation cell gates access to the lending flow. Using mocked verification, to prove the on-chain mechanics independently of any specific KYC provider.
  • Loan Cycle: The full fixed-term lifecycle (deposit, borrow, repay, release) is implemented and tested on CKB testnet.

Technical Architecture

Pipeline

RWA Asset → KYC Attestation → Deposit → Borrow → Repay → Release

Components

Component Location Description
RWA Asset asset/ On-chain representation of a single real-world claim (invoice), implemented as a unique Cell (Type-ID pattern), not a fungible token. Identity is derived from a hash of a consumed input cell’s outpoint at creation time, which guarantees the claim can be issued exactly once and never duplicated. After issuance, the Type Script allows simple transfers (one input, one output) without re-checking uniqueness; authorization is handled by the Lock Script.
KYC Attestation kyc-attestation/ A Cell recording a verification result (subject’s lock hash, status, issued timestamp), written under the issuer’s own Lock Script so only the issuer can revoke it. No custom Type Script is needed for this component: standard Lock Script control is sufficient, since the issuer alone creates and can invalidate the attestation. Verification itself is mocked in the current stage and will be replaced by a live Sumsub integration under this grant.
Lending lending/ A fixed-term deposit/borrow/repay/release state machine. This is the one component with on-chain enforcement logic beyond standard Cell/Lock behavior: the deposit step checks that both the correct RWA asset Cell and a valid, matching, non-revoked KYC attestation Cell are present among the transaction’s inputs before allowing a loan to proceed.

Trust model for this phase

  • On-chain ownership: The RWA claim is represented by a unique CKB Cell controlled by an owner’s Lock Script. The holder can therefore own and transfer the on-chain representation of the claim using native CKB transactions.
  • The RWA asset Cell alone does not imply custody or legal backing of the underlying real-world claim.
  • The lending flow has no price oracle or liquidation logic. Loan terms are fixed at deposit time, which removes the need for live pricing or collateral-ratio monitoring.

Design rationale

Unique Cell instead of a fungible token. The RWA claim (an invoice) is a single, one-of-a-kind item, not a divisible quantity. An earlier version of this project modeled it as a fixed-supply fungible token, which was the wrong fit: there is no meaningful “amount” of one invoice. The Type-ID pattern (uniqueness derived from a consumed input cell’s outpoint) is a well-established CKB technique for exactly this case, used by CKB’s own Type ID script and NFT standards like Spore.

Fixed-term loans instead of a dynamic CDP. A collateralized-debt-position model (like Stable++, an existing live protocol on CKB) requires live pricing and a liquidation engine, real financial-engineering surface area. Since the goal here is building the compliance-gated lending pattern, not building a second CDP protocol, loan terms are fixed at deposit time instead, which removes the need for a price oracle entirely.

A dedicated attestation Cell instead of reusing an existing identity primitive. CKB already has a general-purpose claim/identity system (did:ckb), but its claims are revocable only by the credential holder, not the issuer. That fits reputation use cases well but doesn’t fit compliance: a KYC credential needs to be revocable by the verifying party. This project uses a small, purpose-built attestation Cell instead, rather than retrofitting a primitive built for a different trust model.

Fee Model and Sustainability

The open-source contracts, scripts, and documentation funded by this grant remain free for any CKB project to use. Revenue comes from the production layer built on top of them: a small origination fee on each loan once the platform is live with real loans, and managed onboarding for asset issuers who want a supported integration. Additional revenue can come from paid integration and compliance support for CKB projects that adopt the attestation and unique-asset patterns. As adoption grows, these fees allow the platform to sustain itself without compromising the free, open-source core.

Alignment with CKB philosophy

CKB’s Cell model is well suited to representing a single non-fungible real-world claim with provable uniqueness and explicit ownership. This project uses the Cell model as designed rather than simulating account-based balances.

The RWA application is therefore one use case for a more fundamental primitive: a unique, ownable, transferable on-chain representation of a real-world claim.

Background and Experience

Kirea Finance is built and maintained by Salmandev, I’m a full-stack blockchain developer. My public GitHub (salmansarwarr (Salman Sarwar) · GitHub) holds work across smart contracts and full-stack applications. I have previously completed a project funded under the Nervos Spark program: a “Stripe-Style” React Payment Library for Fiber Network.

For this proposal, I designed and implemented all three core components of Kirea Finance: the Type-ID RWA asset cell, the issuer-revocable KYC attestation cell, and the fixed-term lending state machine. The contracts are written in Rust and compiled for CKB’s RISC-V VM, and the full lifecycle is deployed and verified on CKB testnet.

What This Grant Adds

| Milestone | Deliverable |

|—|—|

| **1. Security hardening, attestation and asset pattern** | Enforce the loan rules on every collateral spend, verify actual net disbursement and repayment, then generalize the attestation cell and asset representation. Details below. |

| **2.Reference KYC integration** |replace mocked verification with a real Sumsub integration that other CKB projects can reuse: webhook handling, mapping results to the on-chain attestation write, sandbox-to-limited-production setup. |

| **3. Repayment edge cases, reference UI and verification tooling** | Explicit late-repayment/default handling on top of the existing repay/release flow; a UI for the lending flow and reference asset (collateral/loan status, lifecycle progress, reproducible testnet activity); expanded testnet verification tooling. |

**Milestone 1 details**

- Enforce the loan rules on every collateral spend: replace the issuer-key vault with a dedicated vault lock that pins the loan type script and only allows the collateral to be spent in a transaction that also consumes the matching loan cell, so the release checks always run.

- Verify actual net disbursement and repayment: borrow and repay compare each party’s token balance across inputs and outputs, so only a real net transfer of at least the loan amount or repay amount passes, not recycled change.

- Tests covering both: a collateral spend without the loan cell must fail, borrow and repay transactions that only recycle the party’s own tokens must fail, and the honest paths still pass.

- Then generalize the attestation cell and asset representation: configurable parameters, documented schema. This lays the groundwork for more asset types in a future phase.

**Acceptance:** the negative tests pass in the test suite, and the updated contracts complete a full deposit-to-release run on testnet.

Budget

Total requested: $7,250 USD equivalent

Area Amount
Attestation + asset pattern hardening (tests, config-driven design) $2,500
Live Sumsub integration (engineering + API/sandbox-to-production fees) $2,500
Repayment handling, UI, and testnet deployment/verification tooling $2,250

Disbursement: staged, 20% ($1,450) on approval, remaining 80% ($5,800) released against milestone completion.

Out of Scope (this phase)

  • Real custody or legal backing of the underlying asset
  • Dynamic collateral ratios, price oracles, or liquidation auctions
  • Mainnet deployment or production issuance
  • General-purpose identity/reputation infrastructure
  • Formal third-party security audit
  • Legal/compliance licensing work

Why This Matters for Nervos

Real-world borrowers need capital, and DeFi has capital looking for yield. Today there is no compliant, on-chain path connecting the two on CKB. Tokenizing real-world assets is increasingly seen as a major direction for the blockchain industry, CKB already has the infrastructure for DeFi applications, but the ecosystem has limited access to high-quality real-world assets and productive external liquidity. This pattern is a first step toward changing that.

This grant turns a working demo into reusable infrastructure:

  • For builders: a documented, configurable attestation Cell and unique-asset pattern, usable for any compliance-gated flow, not just lending.
  • For reviewers and users: explicit late-repayment and default handling, a UI, and reproducible testnet activity that anyone can verify.
  • For the ecosystem: a fully open-source reference showing a bridge-free, custodian-free RWA lending flow on the Cell model.

What this could be used for (future applications, not deliverables of this grant)

  • Invoice and receivables financing. A business borrows against a verified invoice instead of waiting 60–90 days for payment.
  • **Cheaper credit for underserved borrowers.**Producers of physical goods (coffee, commodities, etc.) in places with no access to normal credit can post their real-world assets as collateral, get verified through an on-chain ID+KYC system, and borrow money from DeFi lenders around the world at reasonable rates, instead of going to loan sharks charging predatory interest.
  • Asset-backed short-term loans. Equipment, inventory, or commodity claims used as collateral for fixed-term loans with ability to onboard other types of assets in the future, such as Gold, Real estate, stocks etc.
  • Transferable RWA claims. A uniquely identified claim could potentially be transferred between parties on CKB, subject to the legal and contractual framework governing the underlying real-world asset.

Why on-chain RWA matters (what this pattern enables in future phases)

  • For asset holders: a business or individual holding a real-world claim, such as an invoice, can unlock liquidity from it without selling it, while keeping ownership of the underlying claim.
  • For lenders and liquidity providers: loans backed by verified real-world claims could offer yield sourced from real economic activity, rather than only from crypto-native lending and trading. Yield levels would depend on loan terms and asset quality, and none are promised here.
  • For CKB: access to real-world assets and external liquidity that the ecosystem currently lacks, brought in through a transparent, on-chain lifecycle rather than a bridge or custodian.

Risk & Mitigation

  • Execution risk (solo developer): mitigated by narrow scope and a complete, working demo on testnet before this proposal. I have a previous history of completing projects under the Nervos Spark program. Asset issuance, KYC attestation, deposit, borrow, repay, and release are all implemented and tested, which demonstrates the core pattern is technically sound.
  • KYC vendor dependency: Sumsub is a widely used, established provider; this grant’s integration work is limited to API/webhook integration, not building verification logic from scratch. While also allowing for any KYC to be used without changes to the core design.
  • Scope creep risk: explicitly bounded by the Out of Scope list above.

Call to Action

The core pattern, a real-world claim, gated by KYC, used as loan collateral, is fully implemented and verified end to end on CKB testnet. This proposal funds hardening that working, open-source pattern so any builders, asset type or team can pick it up and extend it.

I appreciate the community’s consideration and welcome any feedback on the architecture, scope, or budget.

item.title: CKB Off Chain Aba: Event Overview
item.dc:creator: Jedi_dtechmaker
item.description:
On October 3, 2026, we brought CKB Off Chain to Aba, Abia State. We worked closely with Abia Web3 Network to make this happen. The weather was terrible, it rained heavily for most of the day, but the people who showed up were exactly the right ones.

Setting the Foundation

I kicked things off by breaking down what CKB actually is and why anyone should care. We didn’t just jump into code. We talked about why blockchain was created in the first place and how CKB stays true to those roots. We covered the Cell Model, explaining it like sealed envelopes, so even people without a blockchain background could understand. I also introduced RGB++ and Fiber Network and what they mean for payments and apps.

Opportunities for Developers

I also shared how developers can plug into this ecosystem. Through the CKBuilders program, there are hackathons, weekly tasks, and opportunities to get funded for building cool stuff. It is not locked behind closed doors. You do not need a degree or a corporate job. If you have the skills and you want to build, there is a way to get support.

Builder Spotlights

The heart of the meetup was the builder presentations. Several local contributors took the stage to share their work and experiences.

  • RIVET presented by myself @Jedi_dtechmaker . RIVET is a tool I built to back up GitHub history onto CKB, IPFS, and Arweave. The problem is simple. Right now, your GitHub profile can be wiped out overnight. RIVET acts like an insurance policy, making sure your work and your reputation on chain can never be deleted.

  • CKB IDL presented by @OWK50GA He explained that building transactions on CKB can sometimes be a headache because there is no clear manual for what a script expects. CKB IDL solves this by creating a standard way to describe and validate data before it hits the chain.

  • FreightOnNervos (FON) presented by @Birdmannn . He introduced a system where every transaction is treated as a deliverable. Individual transactions are called “goods” or “services”, and they usually involve payments like tipping, raffles, or proposals. The overarching system that delivers these goods is called a “freight”. The main innovation is that FON lets you set social criteria and constraints that govern how these payments are executed. You can even use one freight as a condition for another. Beyond his presentation, he also took the time to explain the Nervos Network to newcomers and onboarded several developers right there at the event.

These sessions were not just about showing off work. They sparked conversations and gave attendees a chance to ask questions and engage directly with the builders in the room.

Connections and Outcomes

The best part of the day was the connections. People did not just sit and listen, they actually talked to each other and exchanged ideas. I met several developers who are ready to start building on CKB, which is what this was all about.

Aba in Context

Aba is a city of makers. The people here know how to build things from the ground up and make them work. That is exactly why bringing CKB here makes sense. We have a growing community of developers who are ready to take on new challenges.

I wanted to show them that CKB is a tool they can use to create their own solutions. We do not have to wait for things to happen somewhere else. We can build them right here at home. This meetup was about planting that seed and showing local builders what is possible.

What We Learned and What Comes Next

The rain definitely affected turnout, but we also learned we need to start marketing earlier next time. We will partner with more local groups in Aba and host hands on buildathons where developers can actually code together. This is not a one off. We are going to keep this momentum going.


Conclusion

Aba has a lot of potential. This event was just a glimpse of what is possible. Thank you to Abia Web3 Network for the partnership, and to everyone who came out in the rain. We are just getting started.
