item.title: Spark Program | LiquidLane: Fiber Receive Capacity Marketplace | RESUBMISSION
item.dc:creator: Fidelcoder
item.description:
1. Project Overview

LiquidLane is a CKB-native marketplace where merchants and applications obtain Fiber receive capacity from independent node operators. Providers publish capacity and opening fees, fund channels from their own wallets, and retain their keys. Merchants choose an offer, verify delivery, and pay the provider directly.

The product brings provider discovery, channel provisioning, delivery verification, and fee tracking into one workflow.

2. Team Profile

FidelCoder — Developer and maintainer. Responsible for LiquidLane’s Rust backend, local connector, and Next.js application, with hands-on experience building CKB transaction flows, JoyID authentication, and Fiber channel integrations.

Contact Details

  • GitHub: FidelCoder (Fidel) · GitHub

  • Core repository: GitHub - FidelCoder/liquidlane-core: Backend service for vault accounting, liquidity requests, Fiber channel deployment, and fee distribution on LiquidLane. · GitHub

  • App repository: GitHub - FidelCoder/liquidlane-app: Web app for managing stablecoin liquidity vaults, channel capacity requests, and LP yield on LiquidLane. · GitHub

  • Web interface: https://liquidlane-app.vercel.app

  • Initial Proposal: LiquidLane: LP-Backed Fiber Channel Liquidity

3. Project Background

A working wallet or checkout does not automatically mean a merchant can receive Fiber payments. Receiving requires sufficient channel capacity funded by peers toward the merchant. CKB held in the merchant’s own wallet does not, by itself, provide that capacity. An application can therefore be correctly integrated while customer payments still fail because the receiving path lacks liquidity.

This creates a coordination problem on both sides. Merchants and application developers need to find funded peers, compare terms, and establish when receiving capacity is usable. Node operators need a way to advertise available capital, set prices and funding limits, and reach customers who need it.

Channel creation provides the underlying mechanism. A usable capacity market also needs discovery, clear service terms, delivery evidence, and payment records. LiquidLane brings those pieces together so acquiring receive capacity becomes a repeatable service for CKB wallets, merchant tools, and payment applications.

4. Solution

LiquidLane makes a defined amount of usable receive capacity available as a priced service. Providers publish how much they can supply and the opening fee they charge. Merchants can compare offers, understand the capital required by their receiving node, and choose terms suited to their payment needs.

Each purchase has an agreement signed by both parties, binding the participants, capacity, funding amount, fee recipient, and opening deadline. A local connector enforces the provider’s funding limits before committing capital. This makes provisioning repeatable while keeping spending authority with the node operator.

Delivery checks combine committed channel funding, matching observations from both nodes, and a paid test invoice. The agreed capacity must remain available after the test payment. A signed receipt records the agreement and delivery evidence, while fee tracking distinguishes paid, outstanding, and waived amounts.

Supply comes from operators committing their own capital to native bidirectional channels. They set their prices and earn opening fees and any routing fees actually received. Merchants pay for receiving capability and retain their incoming payments. LiquidLane gives these parties a common service agreement and operational record while native Fiber handles payment routing and settlement.

5. Technical Approach

The system combines a Rust/Axum coordinator, SQLite persistence, a local Rust connector, and a Next.js/TypeScript interface with JoyID signing. The release targets native CKB on testnet and Fiber 0.9.0.

Fund control: the coordinator holds no participant signing keys. Each connector independently checks signatures, funding limits, peer identity, and agreed fees. The node negotiates native channel funding and supplies its own closing destination. Funding and settlement use Fiber’s native CKB scripts.

Capacity accounting: a 500 CKB offer requires a 600 CKB provider contribution: 500 usable capacity, 99 native reserve, and 1 for the delivery probe. The merchant funds its own reserve, and both wallets need transaction headroom. These amounts are itemized before acceptance.

Payments and recovery: customer payments move through native Fiber channels. The provider receives corresponding value in its incoming channel; the merchant owns received payments. Existing payments and native closure remain available if the coordinator stops. Recovery follows Fiber’s settlement rules and delays, with confirmed wallet outputs checked separately from channel status.

Service boundaries: this product sells initial capacity. It does not guarantee duration or replenishment. Fees follow delivery and can remain unpaid; local limits bound provider exposure. Participants remain responsible for securing their node keys and current channel state.

6. To-Do List

Milestone 1 — Marketplace and onboarding improvements · Weeks 1–2

  • Week 1: package connector releases with checksums and installation instructions; add setup diagnostics for pairing, connectivity, service startup, and funding readiness.

  • Week 2: add offer filtering by capacity, fee, and availability; implement offer renewal while preserving accepted quotes; improve mobile onboarding.

Completion: an operator can install the packaged connector, diagnose setup problems, and publish or renew an offer. A merchant can find a suitable provider through the improved interface.

Milestone 2 — Reliability and beta release · Weeks 3–4

  • Week 3: add actionable recovery guidance for interrupted setup, uncertain payments, and pending settlement; introduce order/fee activity exports and activation metrics.

  • Week 4: automate coordinator backups and verify restoration; restore hosted API connectivity and persistent storage; test machine reboot, fresh-node JoyID funding, and interruption recovery.

Completion: publish a usable testnet release with working hosted services, documented recovery procedures, and passing checks that retries do not duplicate funding or payments. The market beta begins after this milestone.

Milestone 3 — Market beta and product iteration · Weeks 5–6

  • Week 5: recruit 30–40 beta participants through Nervos/Fiber communities and direct outreach to operators, merchants, and wallet/application builders. Target at least three independently operated providers.

  • Week 6: address beta defects, refine onboarding, and publish results covering usability, transaction completion, provider economics, and repeat-use interest.

Completion targets: 30–40 participants completing a role-specific workflow and feedback; at least ten completed capacity purchases across independent providers; a released update addressing reported issues. Report registrations, active participants, completed purchases, and failed or unpaid orders separately.

7. Required Funding & Funding Breakdown

Total requested: $1,000 USD.

  • Milestone 1 — $350: $300 for onboarding and marketplace development; $50 for connector packaging and installation documentation.

  • Milestone 2 — $350: $250 for reliability improvements and recovery testing; $100 for hosting, domain, and monitoring.

  • Milestone 3 — $300: $100 for recruitment and onboarding support; $100 for structured usability sessions and feedback collection; $100 for product fixes and the completion report.

Funding supports development, deployment, and participant testing. Node capital remains participant-controlled. An external security audit and mainnet deployment are outside this scope.

8. Deliverables + How to Verify

  • M1: packaged connector and improved marketplace. Install the published release on Linux x86_64, follow the setup guide, publish/renew an offer, and filter available capacity. Provide binaries, checksums, source changes, and a short walkthrough.

  • M2: hosted testnet release and recovery package. Open the app and health endpoint, complete a purchase, and inspect its funding, probe, and fee evidence. Publish restart, backup/restore, and payment-retry results with expected outputs.

  • M3: beta release and results report. Publish participant totals, completed workflows, transaction references, feedback, costs, and resolved issues. Count participants once; project-operated nodes do not count as independent providers.

Reviewers can inspect recordings, receipts, and explorer links without running nodes. Live reproduction requires compatible Fiber nodes, a CKB RPC/indexer, testnet funds, and a separate payer route. Build instructions specify Rust 1.91 and Node 22.

Verification guides:

  • Connector setup: liquidlane-core/docs/automatic-provider-setup.md at main · FidelCoder/liquidlane-core · GitHub

  • Operations and recovery: liquidlane-core/docs/marketplace-operations.md at main · FidelCoder/liquidlane-core · GitHub

9. Current State vs. Funded Work

Already implemented: wallet authentication, node pairing, signed quotes, local funding limits, durable orders, automatic channel opening, delivery checks, direct fees, and merchant/provider interfaces. Both repositories use the MIT license.

Demonstrated: automatic delivery of 500 CKB, a routed probe, a confirmed opening fee, one real JoyID purchase, and outage/recovery verification. These used project-operated nodes. The normal Rust suite passes 88 tests, with two additional tests ignored.

Evidence:

  • Automatic capacity delivery: liquidlane-core/docs/evidence/automatic-capacity at main · FidelCoder/liquidlane-core · GitHub

  • Provider funding: liquidlane-core/docs/evidence/provider-funding at main · FidelCoder/liquidlane-core · GitHub

  • Payments during coordinator outage: liquidlane-core/docs/evidence/coordinator-outage at main · FidelCoder/liquidlane-core · GitHub

  • Settlement and service recovery: liquidlane-core/docs/evidence/settlement-recovery at main · FidelCoder/liquidlane-core · GitHub

Funded additions: packaged connector distribution, setup diagnostics, offer filtering/renewal, recovery guidance, activity exports, automated backups, and hosted-release improvements, followed by the participant testing specified in Milestone 3. Hosted API restoration, full reboot testing, and JoyID funding of a newly managed node remain pending.

10. CKB Alignment

LiquidLane connects Fiber’s native channels with CKB settlement and JoyID wallet signing. Its open-source connector, marketplace API, and delivery receipts give CKB developers reusable components for acquiring receive capacity. This supports wallet and checkout integrations while keeping channel operation and capital under participant control

item.title: FiberNuts Community Market: A Testnet App for Cashu + Fiber
item.dc:creator: Code3ks
item.description:
Gm CKB community,

In my earlier FiberNuts post, I said the next step should be more than improving the wallet. It should be a high-level application that shows why Cashu + Fiber could be useful in an everyday setting.

That application is now built: FiberNuts Community Market.

The idea is a small community event where attendees can buy items or tip contributors with RUSD ecash, while vendors receive and secure those payments before cashing out through Fiber.

Fiber moves RUSD into and out of the system. Cashu handles the many lightweight payments in between.

What the demo looks like

The application has two separate experiences:

  • Attendee: market.fibernuts.xyz
  • Vendor terminal: market.fibernuts.xyz/vendor

A complete payment works like this:

  1. The attendee adds RUSD ecash by paying a Fiber invoice.
  2. The vendor selects an item, such as a 2.50 RUSD coffee, and creates a payment request.
  3. The attendee scans one QR code and reviews the amount, mint, fee, and remaining balance before paying.
  4. The attendee wallet creates a Cashu payment locked to the vendor’s key and delivers it through the payment relay.
  5. The vendor stores the received payment, checks it with the issuing mint, and swaps it for fresh proofs.
  6. The order becomes Paid only after those fresh proofs are stored in the vendor balance.
  7. The vendor can later cash out by asking the mint to pay an external RUSD Fiber invoice.

The distinction in step 6 is important. Delivered means the payment reached the vendor flow; it does not mean settlement is complete. The vendor sees Paid only after the issuing mint accepts the proofs and returns fresh ones.

What was added beyond the wallet

This is a focused event-payment application rather than another general wallet dashboard. It includes:

  • A vendor catalog, order builder, QR checkout, current order, and order history.
  • A one-scan NUT-18 payment flow with an exact review screen before value moves.
  • Vendor-key locking so the delivery relay cannot redeem the payment itself.
  • Separate attendee and vendor balances and operation histories.
  • Add-cash and cash-out flows that use Fiber at the boundaries.
  • Recovery states for interrupted delivery, settlement, issuance, and cash-out operations.
  • Persistent network, asset, mint, and testnet identification throughout the interface.

The trust boundary is still visible

This demo does not change the underlying Cashu trust model. The mint remains custodial and controls issuance, swaps, and redemption. Browser storage is not a secure backup, mint availability does not prove solvency, and a user still needs a funded RUSD Fiber route to add cash or cash out.

The current vendor-locked payment also has no attendee refund path after confirmation. That makes the relay unable to spend the payment, but it means this version should be used only with small testnet values while refund semantics are designed and tested properly.

The goal is not to hide these boundaries. It is to show a practical application while making the exact moment of settlement and the remaining custodial risk understandable.

What I would like feedback on

  1. Does the attendee-and-vendor flow make the role of Cashu + Fiber clearer than the standalone wallet?
  2. Would a community event or meetup be a useful place to test this with several attendees and vendors?
  3. What information should a user see before accepting ecash from a mint?
  4. What recovery or refund behavior would you require before using this beyond a controlled testnet demo?

The source is available at github.com/code3ks/fibernuts. The application, mint, and payment relay are deployed for use with CKB testnet, but please treat them as experimental infrastructure and use test value only.

item.title: Spark Program | DAO Cycle Alerts: Telegram reminders before your Nervos DAO cycle ends
item.dc:creator: yukikawata
item.description:
English

1. Project overview

  • Name: DAO Cycle Alerts
  • One line: A read-only Telegram bot and CLI that tell Nervos DAO depositors when each deposit’s 180-epoch cycle is about to end, so they start a withdrawal in time and do not lose another 30 days.
  • Type: user tool (Telegram bot) plus developer tool (npm package and CLI).

2. Team profile

  • Yuki Kawata: sole developer and maintainer.
  • Past work: TheYukiKawata (Yuki Kawata) · GitHub (ton-checkout, arc-tabs, arc-till: payment tools on TON and Arc, deployed on Cloudflare Workers).
  • Contact: yuki@yukikawata.fyi (email only).

3. Project background

A Nervos DAO deposit unlocks only at the end of a 180-epoch cycle, about 30 days (RFC 23). You can start a withdrawal (phase 1) at any time, but the CKB stays locked until the current cycle ends. The deposit also stops earning compensation from that moment.

So the best time to start phase 1 is a few hours before the cycle ends. If you miss it by a day, the deposit rolls into a new cycle and you wait about 30 more days.

Today you find out where your deposit sits in its cycle only by opening Neuron or another wallet and checking. Nothing tells you ahead of time. There are 16,696 depositors holding 8.12 billion CKB in the DAO (CKB Explorer, 2026-09-26). Many of them hold long term and do not open a wallet every week.

Scenario: Li deposited 50,000 CKB in March and wants the CKB back for a purchase in October. She opens Neuron on October 3, starts the withdrawal, and learns that the cycle ended on October 1. The CKB unlocks on October 31.

4. Solution

  • In Telegram, the user sends /watch <ckb address>. The bot lists each DAO deposit with its cycle end time.
  • The bot sends a message 3 days and 12 hours before each cycle end: “Deposit of 50,000 CKB (tx 0xab..): cycle ends in about 12 hours (epoch 9123, around 2026-10-01 14:00 UTC). Start the withdrawal in your wallet before then to unlock at that time.”
  • For deposits already in phase 1, the bot sends a message when phase 2 becomes possible: “Your withdrawing deposit can be unlocked now.”
  • /list shows every watched deposit. /forget deletes the address and chat data.
  • The bot never asks for keys, signatures or wallet connections. It reads public chain data only.
  • Differences from existing tools: wallets show a countdown only while you have them open. This tool sends the reminder to you, and it works for any address, including cold wallets and multisig.

5. Technical approach

  • Language: TypeScript. Runtime: Cloudflare Workers with a cron trigger every 30 minutes. Storage: Cloudflare D1 (chat id, address, sent reminders).
  • Chain data: CKB public RPC and indexer (get_cells filtered by the Nervos DAO type script and the user’s lock script, get_header for deposit epochs, get_tip_header for the current epoch).
  • Core library dao-cycle (built, see section 9), on top of CCC:
    • find the address’s Nervos DAO cells and classify them as deposited (data is 8 zero bytes) or withdrawing (data is the deposit block number);
    • compute the unlock epoch with the DAO script’s own rule (c/dao.c): count the epochs from deposit to withdrawal, round up to a multiple of 180 (at least 180), add that to the deposit epoch. For a deposited cell the withdrawal epoch is the current tip, so the result is the end of the current cycle;
    • estimate wall-clock time from the average epoch length over the last 300,000 blocks (about 180 epochs).
  • CLI: dao-cycle check <address> prints the same table the bot uses.
  • Hardest part: accurate time estimates, since epoch length changes. The bot states times as “around” and re-checks every 30 minutes, so the 12-hour reminder uses fresh data.
  • Language: English, with Chinese message templates.
  • AI use: code, tests and docs are written with an AI coding agent (Claude).
  • Testing: the unlock epoch math is covered by tests, including RFC 23’s example transaction, and was checked against CCC’s calcDaoClaimEpoch on 150 mainnet withdrawing cells.

6. To-do list

  • Week 1: Telegram bot on Cloudflare Workers. /watch, /list, /forget, D1 storage, cron job. Milestone: bot answers /watch on mainnet.
  • Week 2: Reminders. 3-day and 12-hour messages, “ready to unlock” message, reminder de-duplication, Chinese and English messages, simulate command. Milestone: reminders live, dao-cycle published to npm.
  • Week 3: Seed users. Announce on Nervos Talk and CKB community channels. Target: 20 watched addresses. Collect feedback and fix issues.
  • Week 4: Completion report: usage numbers, reminders sent, feedback, fund usage.

7. Required funding and breakdown

  • Total: $1,000, paid in CKB.
  • Technical work (weeks 1 and 2): $700. Bot, reminders, simulate command, npm release, tests, deployment.
  • User testing (weeks 3 and 4): $200. Onboarding seed users, fixes from feedback, completion report.
  • Hosting: $100. Runs on the Cloudflare Workers free tier. This covers a paid tier or a dedicated RPC endpoint if load or rate limits require it, for 12 months after completion.

8. Deliverables and how to verify

Deliverables:

  1. Public GitHub repository (MIT) with the library, CLI and bot.
  2. npm package dao-cycle with the CLI.
  3. Live Telegram bot on mainnet.
  4. Completion report on Nervos Talk.

How to verify (no code review needed):

  1. Unlock math: bun install && bun test. Expected: all tests pass, including the RFC 23 case (deposit at epoch 2+648/1677, withdrawing cell at 47+382/1605, unlock at 182+648/1677).
  2. CLI against real data: bunx dao-cycle check <any address with a DAO deposit>. Expected: one row per deposit with the next cycle end epoch. Compare it with the same address in Neuron or CKB Explorer.
  3. Bot: send /watch <address> to the bot. Expected: the same table within a minute.
  4. Reminder timing without waiting 30 days: bunx dao-cycle simulate <address> --at-epoch <epoch> prints the reminders the bot would send at that epoch.
  5. Privacy: /forget, then /list. Expected: “No addresses watched.”

Environment: Bun 1.x on any OS, internet access, a Telegram account. About 10 minutes in total.

9. Current state and funded work

  • Current state: the core library and CLI work on mainnet: GitHub - TheYukiKawata/dao-cycle: Find when each Nervos DAO deposit on a CKB address reaches the end of its 180-epoch cycle · GitHub (MIT). Run bun install && bun src/cli.ts check <address> to see each DAO cell on an address with its unlock epoch, estimated time and time left. Tests pass in CI, including the RFC 23 example. The unlock math gave the same result as CCC’s calcDaoClaimEpoch on the 150 newest withdrawing cells on mainnet.
  • Funded work: the Telegram bot, reminders, simulate command, npm release, seed users and the completion report (sections 6 and 8).

10. CKB alignment

The tool depends on CKB features: the Nervos DAO type script, cell data as the deposit/withdrawing marker, and absolute-epoch since rules. It serves CKB holders directly and keeps DAO deposits from being locked longer than needed. Future work, if the committee wants it after DAO v1.1 settles: reminders for Community Fund DAO votes, since DAO deposits are the voting weight.

中文

1. 项目概述

  • 名称：DAO Cycle Alerts
  • 一句话：一个只读的 Telegram 机器人和命令行工具，在每笔 Nervos DAO 存款的 180 个 epoch 周期即将结束时提醒存款人，让他们及时发起取款，避免再等 30 天。
  • 类型：用户工具（Telegram 机器人）+ 开发者工具（npm 包和 CLI）。

2. 团队简介

  • Yuki Kawata：唯一开发者和维护者。
  • 过往项目：github.com/TheYukiKawata（ton-checkout、arc-tabs、arc-till：基于 TON 和 Arc 的支付工具，部署在 Cloudflare Workers 上）。
  • 联系方式：yuki@yukikawata.fyi（仅限邮件）。

3. 项目背景

Nervos DAO 存款只能在 180 个 epoch（约 30 天）周期结束时解锁（RFC 23）。你可以随时发起取款第一步，但 CKB 会一直锁定到当前周期结束，而且从那一刻起不再获得补偿。

因此，最佳做法是在周期结束前几个小时发起第一步。如果晚了一天，存款会进入新周期，需要再等约 30 天。

目前，想知道存款处于周期的哪个位置，只能打开 Neuron 或其他钱包查看，没有任何工具会提前通知你。Nervos DAO 目前有 16,696 位存款人，存款总额 81.2 亿 CKB（CKB Explorer，2026-09-26）。其中很多人长期持有，并不会每周打开钱包。

场景：Li 在 3 月存入 50,000 CKB，想在 10 月取回用于一笔支出。她在 10 月 3 日打开 Neuron 发起取款，才发现周期已在 10 月 1 日结束，CKB 要到 10 月 31 日才能解锁。

4. 解决方案

  • 用户在 Telegram 发送 /watch <CKB 地址>，机器人列出每笔 DAO 存款及其周期结束时间。
  • 在每个周期结束前 3 天和 12 小时，机器人发送提醒：“50,000 CKB 存款（交易 0xab..）：周期约 12 小时后结束（epoch 9123，约 2026-10-01 14:00 UTC）。请在此之前在钱包中发起取款，届时即可解锁。”
  • 对已处于第一步的存款，当可以执行第二步时，机器人发送：“你的取款中存款现在可以解锁了。”
  • /list 显示所有监控中的存款；/forget 删除地址和聊天数据。
  • 机器人从不索取私钥、签名或钱包连接，只读取公开链上数据。
  • 与现有工具的区别：钱包只有在打开时才显示倒计时；本工具主动推送提醒，并适用于任何地址，包括冷钱包和多签地址。

5. 技术方案

  • 语言：TypeScript。运行环境：Cloudflare Workers，每 30 分钟执行一次定时任务。存储：Cloudflare D1（聊天 ID、地址、已发送的提醒）。
  • 链上数据：CKB 公共 RPC 和索引器（按 Nervos DAO type script 和用户 lock script 调用 get_cells，用 get_header 获取存款 epoch，用 get_tip_header 获取当前 epoch）。
  • 核心库 dao-cycle（已完成，见第 9 节），基于 CCC：
    • 查找地址上的 Nervos DAO cell，并区分存款 cell（data 为 8 个零字节）和取款中 cell（data 为存款区块高度）；
    • 按 DAO 脚本自身的规则（c/dao.c）计算解锁 epoch：统计从存款到取款经过的 epoch 数，向上取整到 180 的倍数（至少 180），再加到存款 epoch 上。对存款 cell，取款 epoch 取当前 tip，因此结果就是当前周期的结束点；
    • 根据最近 300,000 个区块（约 180 个 epoch）的平均 epoch 时长估算实际时间。
  • CLI：dao-cycle check <地址> 输出与机器人相同的表格。
  • 难点：epoch 时长会变化，时间估算需要准确。机器人以“约”表述时间，并每 30 分钟重新计算，确保 12 小时提醒使用最新数据。
  • 语言：英文，附中文消息模板。
  • AI 使用：代码、测试和文档借助 AI 编程代理（Claude）编写。
  • 测试：解锁 epoch 计算有测试覆盖（包括 RFC 23 的示例交易），并已在 150 个主网取款中 cell 上与 CCC 的 calcDaoClaimEpoch 对照。

6. 执行计划

  • 第 1 周：部署在 Cloudflare Workers 上的 Telegram 机器人。/watch、/list、/forget、D1 存储、定时任务。里程碑：机器人在主网上响应 /watch。
  • 第 2 周：提醒功能。3 天和 12 小时提醒、“可以解锁”提醒、提醒去重、中英文消息、simulate 命令。里程碑：提醒上线，dao-cycle 发布到 npm。
  • 第 3 周：种子用户。在 Nervos Talk 和 CKB 社区频道发布。目标：20 个监控地址。收集反馈并修复问题。
  • 第 4 周：结项报告：使用数据、已发送提醒数、用户反馈、资金使用情况。

7. 所需资金与明细

  • 总额：1,000 美元，以 CKB 支付。
  • 技术开发（第 1、2 周）：700 美元。机器人、提醒、simulate 命令、npm 发布、测试、部署。
  • 用户测试（第 3、4 周）：200 美元。种子用户引导、根据反馈修复、结项报告。
  • 托管：100 美元。项目运行在 Cloudflare Workers 免费套餐上；若负载或速率限制需要，用于结项后 12 个月内的付费套餐或专用 RPC。

8. 交付物与验证方式

交付物：

  1. 公开 GitHub 仓库（MIT 协议），包含库、CLI 和机器人。
  2. npm 包 dao-cycle（含 CLI）。
  3. 主网上线的 Telegram 机器人。
  4. Nervos Talk 上的结项报告。

验证方式（无需审查代码）：

  1. 解锁计算：bun install && bun test。预期：全部测试通过，包括 RFC 23 用例（存款于 epoch 2+648/1677，取款中 cell 于 47+382/1605，解锁于 182+648/1677）。
  2. 真实数据：bunx dao-cycle check <任意有 DAO 存款的地址>。预期：每笔存款一行，显示下一个周期结束 epoch。可在 Neuron 或 CKB Explorer 中对照同一地址。
  3. 机器人：向机器人发送 /watch <地址>。预期：一分钟内返回相同表格。
  4. 无需等待 30 天验证提醒时机：bunx dao-cycle simulate <地址> --at-epoch <epoch> 输出机器人在该 epoch 会发送的提醒。
  5. 隐私：发送 /forget 后再发送 /list。预期：“没有监控中的地址。”

环境：任意系统上的 Bun 1.x、网络连接、一个 Telegram 账号。总计约 10 分钟。

9. 当前状态与资助范围

  • 当前状态：核心库和 CLI 已可在主网上使用：https://github.com/TheYukiKawata/dao-cycle（MIT 协议）。运行 bun install && bun src/cli.ts check <地址>，即可查看该地址上每个 DAO cell 的解锁 epoch、预计时间和剩余时间。CI 中测试全部通过，包括 RFC 23 示例。解锁计算在主网最新的 150 个取款中 cell 上与 CCC 的 calcDaoClaimEpoch 结果一致。
  • 资助范围：Telegram 机器人、提醒功能、simulate 命令、npm 发布、种子用户和结项报告（第 6、8 节）。

10. CKB 契合度

本工具依赖 CKB 的特性：Nervos DAO type script、以 cell data 区分存款与取款中状态、以及绝对 epoch 的 since 规则。它直接服务 CKB 持有者，避免 DAO 存款被多锁一个周期。后续方向（如委员会在 DAO v1.1 稳定后有需要）：为社区基金 DAO 投票发送提醒，因为 DAO 存款就是投票权重。

item.title: Paying a .cell name over Fiber on testnet: what it took
item.dc:creator: LusoCryptoLabs
item.description:
In early September we checked whether a .cell name can work as a Fiber payment endpoint: a payer reads the name, finds the node, and pays it without asking the payee for anything. On testnet it did, including a payment routed through a public hub. Two things had to be fixed on the payee’s side first, and they are the useful part of this post.

The records

A name publishes two records:

  • fiber.node: the node’s public key, 33 raw bytes. Fiber’s RPC takes it as bare hex in target_pubkey, so strip any 0x prefix at that boundary.
  • fiber.addr: a multiaddr, as text.

There is no invoice record. An invoice is made for one payment, so the payer keysends to the published key, or asks for an invoice out of band. A wrong or stale key is a denial of payment, not a theft: payments settle against the node key, so publishing someone else’s key sends the money to them.

The records for telmo.cell went on chain in 0xba70f36da3101ef7439fbc417351f714ca04bcc629d37d481808764446a713a1, Pudge block 22301240, 2026-09-03 22:27 UTC. Like every record, they sit in the witness and the cell commits to their hash.

What we measured

In every step the payee was addressed only by the key read back from the name.

Step Result
Dial A node with no bootnodes dialled the published multiaddr and completed the handshake in about 3 s. The payee logged the inbound peer from a public IP.
Direct keysend, 1.23 CKB Success, fee 0, no invoice. Payee +123,000,000 shannons, payer -123,000,000.
Routed keysend, 2.34 CKB To a node the payer had no channel with: Success, fee 234,000 shannons (0.1%).
Pay by name, 4.56 CKB An independent node, with its own identity and network, one channel to a public hub and no channel to the payee, resolved telmo.cell and paid it: Success, fee 456,000 shannons (0.1%), payee +456,000,000 exactly.

The fee is how we know the payments were forwarded. A direct channel costs 0, and each routed payment cost exactly the hub’s advertised tlc_fee_proportional_millionths, 1000.

The payments themselves are off chain. The evidence is each node’s payment status and channel balances, which we logged. The only on-chain part is the records’ transaction above.

What had to be true first

  1. A private channel makes the node invisible. The payee’s only channel was private, so it did not appear in graph_nodes and no other node could compute a route to it. The name resolved perfectly to a node the network could not see.
  2. A new channel is outbound only. A public 2000 CKB channel to a hub still could not receive, because the other side held nothing pointing back. The payee had to spend 200 CKB out through it first. After that it held an announced 1901 CKB channel with about 200 CKB of inbound liquidity, which was the most a single routed payment into the name could carry.

So being payable is something the node operator arranges, not something a name declares.

Limits

  • This was testnet, between 3 and 4 September. The namespace it ran on was replaced by a new deployment on 4 September, and the payee node is no longer running, so the exact setup cannot be re-run. The record format is unchanged.
  • Today no name publishes a Fiber node: 0 of 62 on mainnet and 0 of 43 on testnet, checked on 2026-09-27.
  • Paying over Fiber needs a running fnn node. We know of no end-user wallet that pays Fiber today, so this is for node operators and services, not for a person with a phone.

Trying it

A name’s records come back from GET https://cellula.id/api/resolve/<name> (or testnet.cellula.id) with a fiber field, null when the name publishes none. From there it is a send_payment on your own node, with target_pubkey set to the key without 0x, and keysend: true.

If you run a Fiber node and want to try paying a name, or see a better endpoint to publish than a key and a multiaddr, say so here.

item.title: Cellula.id: `.cell` names on CKB, with the contracts public and reproducible
item.dc:creator: LusoCryptoLabs
item.description:
Cellula.id,.cell is a naming protocol on CKB, live on mainnet since 21 September. A name is one live cell under a fixed type script; its records ride in the witness and the cell commits to their
hash. The product story, why a name here can be paid in ways an ENS name cannot, is on Scryve: A name you can be paid at | Scryve .

The type script cannot check a signature

account-cell-type verifies no signature and has no code that could. Every account cell sits
under a uniform always-success lock, so the type script is the only guardian, and it runs on
inputs and outputs alike. Ownership is a lock hash in the cell’s data. An owner action
(edit, delegate, transfer, sell) is proven by spending, in the same transaction, a cell under
that lock. Which algorithm that lock runs is the lock’s business.

Two things fall out of that:

  • Every lock CKB has works today, and every lock CKB gets later works without a release from us. JoyID, secp256k1, OmniLock, a passkey.
  • A name can be owned by sphincs-all-in-one-lock today. We ran the whole loop countless times: transfer to a SPHINCS+ owner, delegate an everyday manager, edit from the manager, transfer back. The contract was not changed for it; the app grew a screen. The footnote belongs in the same paragraph: on mainnet that lock is a type-id cell under a multisig that is not ours, so the resolver fingerprints the deployed code every ten minutes and the app refuses to protect a name while the fingerprint differs.

The other way to support many wallets is a verifier per scheme compiled into the script. We put that question in the lock, where the cell model already answers it, so nothing on our side has to grow when a new wallet appears

Registration is permissionless, and the predecessor cannot be harmed

Names are kept unique by a ring: registering x spends the predecessor cell and recreates it
pointing at x. The predecessor belongs to someone else, so a stranger has to be able to
spend it. The type script allows exactly that and nothing else: on register the predecessor
is preserved byte for byte except its next pointer, and its capacity may not shrink. Whoever
drives the transaction can splice in a well-formed name and can do nothing to the neighbour,
which is why no signature is asked of them. Genesis is gated by a one-time token whose type
hash is the namespace id, because a type script cannot see global state.

The arithmetic a percentage fee cannot survive

1% of 100 CKB is 1 CKB. No cell can be 1 CKB, because a cell holds its own bytes, and ours is
63 of them. A small fee is not small here; it is impossible. So the sale lock charges nothing
under 630 CKB, a flat cell up to 6,300, and 1% above. The same reasoning is why the fee in the
contract is a ceiling and not an oracle: a separate price cell may discount it, by at most a
sixteenth every six hours, within a band the contract enforces, and nothing can charge above
the schedule. The keeper that steps it is one key that can move the factor a sixteenth
either way, once every six hours, and never above the ceiling.

What is public, and what is not

  • The contracts: GitHub - LusoCryptoLabs/cells-contracts: The four Nervos CKB scripts behind .cell names: unique, owned, priced, sellable. The mainnet binaries reproduce from this source. · GitHub . Four scripts and a shared
    crate, 182 tests, CI runs make test on every push and a second job rebuilds the mainnet
    binaries and compares hashes. The four data hashes on mainnet:

    • account-cell-type 0xf86bdba9ff22b5018dcb90a22cdb3720cd5ea8868ab94959ac8146a6789aae30

    • account-lock 0xa46c19f2262abc0d0db0de3952b7477792b36b392645e0f60e74637ae3e3f13b

    • sale-lock 0xf1160f64a82e3509211b2903fc54f9f15cbdc4758d058f107608d30727072a93

    • price-cell-type 0x238e74e1d2d5bf8f06f9f4b0bb352c2addd531351a45cfeddf3ff5f6f5662342

    • cellula.id/api/verifyfetches the deployed code and hashes it against these; the answer is JSON, and the same check takes one get_live_cell and one blake2b against any node.

  • The resolver: GitHub - LusoCryptoLabs/cells-resolver: The HTTP read API for .cell names on Nervos CKB, as it runs at cellula.id. Run your own with one docker command. · GitHub , the service as it runs at
    cellula.id/api. docker run -e CKB_NETWORK=mainnet -p 8787:8787 cells-resolver is a complete second instance; there is no database. Every /resolve answer carries the outpoint, the type script and the data hash, so any node can confirm it.

  • The bug classes we met, as toy scripts with failing tests:
    GitHub - LusoCryptoLabs/ckb-script-pitfalls: Ways a Nervos CKB script goes wrong that have each cost somebody something: a toy script and a test per class, accepted as written and refused once fixed · GitHub . Five of them are from these contracts,
    each linked to the real test.

  • The app: its built bytes are on both chains as CKBFS cells under the operator key, and
    cellula.id/developers fetches them back and compares them with what it is running: 66 of 66 files. Its source is private. The upgrade key exists and is stated in TRUST.md rather than hidden; constraining it is the next piece of work. No outside audit yet, by choice.

What we would like from here

  • It is live on mainnet, at cellula.id.
  • Tell us what a wallet needs in order to resolve a name.
  • If you run a resolver, say so. A second one anywhere is a full one.

Questions answered here, same day.

item.title: Fiber Test Lab — local, reproducible failure scenarios for Fiber payments
item.dc:creator: nhkhanq
item.description:
Hi everyone,

I built Fiber Test Lab while trying to learn Fiber, and I’d really value your feedback

It started from a problem I kept hitting: I wanted to write tests for what happens when a payment fails — not enough outbound liquidity, no route, an expired invoice, or a peer that goes offline halfway — and I couldn’t.

Those are exactly the states that you cannot easily force on a shared testnet when you want them.

So I ended up building a tool that makes these scenarios reproducible locally.

fiber-lab up two-hop-route starts real FNN nodes plus a CKB devnet in Docker, opens the channels, runs the payment, checks the outcome, and records every RPC call along the way.

The same scenario, the same pinned versions, and the same result.

That was the whole point.

Install: npm i -D fiber-test-lab

Repository: fiber-test-lab

github.com

GitHub - nhkhanq/fiber-test-lab

Contribute to nhkhanq/fiber-test-lab development by creating an account on GitHub.

The project was built during the “Gone in 60ms” hackathon, and I’ve continued working on it since.

What it does today

A scenario is simply a YAML file that describes the topology and what you expect to happen.

Example:

name: two-hop-bottleneck

nodes: [alice, bob, charlie]

channels:
  - { from: alice, to: bob, capacity: 500 }
  - { from: bob, to: charlie, capacity: 200 }

seed:
  - { action: send_payment, from: alice, to: charlie, amount: 180 }

expect:
  status: failed
  reason: no_route_found

The project currently provides several main features:

  • CLI: fiber-lab up | seed | reset | logs | list | ui — every command supports --json, and the exit codes separate a broken configuration (1) from a Docker/RPC failure (2) from an assertion that didn’t match (3), so CI can tell them apart.

  • Nine scenarios so far: direct channel, two-hop route, insufficient capacity, a bottlenecked middle hop, channel drain, round trip, expired invoice, peer offline, and one paying RUSD over a UDT channel.

  • Vitest test-kit: setupScenario(), expectPaymentSucceeds(), and expectPaymentFails(reason) — so you can assert on this from your own test suite.

  • Isolated runs: every run is isolated by a run-id. The network and containers are all named after it, so two runs in two terminals don’t collide.

  • Complete RPC run-log: every RPC goes into a run-log, including successful calls. After a reset, the containers are gone, so that file is the only record of what happened.

  • Run viewer: fiber-lab ui draws the channels, shows where the balance sits on each one, and displays every RPC call with its timing. It fills in live while a run builds. Screenshots are available in the README.

Things I ran into that might be useful to you

These are the things I’d have liked to know earlier, all against FNN 0.8.0.

Every failure comes back as -32000

So I ended up matching on substrings of the message, which I’m not happy about but couldn’t see a way around.

peer_offline and insufficient_outbound produce the same message

When I killed a peer mid-payment, the error was "max outbound liquidity 0 … insufficient" — word for word what a real liquidity shortage gives you.

I now check list_peers first and only fall back to reading the message.

This one cost me an evening, and I mention it because any tool that reads the message alone will tell you “insufficient liquidity” when your peer is simply gone.

The default gossip interval made my multi-hop tests flaky

At 60 seconds, the route often wasn’t known to the sender yet when the test fired.

I set it to 2000 milliseconds on the devnet nodes, and it became reliable.

Almost all the time is spent waiting for ChannelReady

One measured two-hop run took:

  • 8.8s to build and start the containers

  • 5.4s until they were healthy

  • 40.2s and 39.1s to open the two channels

  • 2.0s for the actual payment

96 seconds in total.

I had assumed Docker was the slow part.

It isn’t.

What’s not done, and I’d rather say so

  • insufficient_inbound, reserve_violation, channel_not_ready, and amount_out_of_range are in my error list, but I haven’t managed to force any of them against a real node yet, so I don’t fully trust them.

  • Devnet isn’t mainnet. Block time, fees, and some limits differ, so this doesn’t replace testing on a real testnet.

  • peer-offline is simulated with docker kill, which isn’t a real network partition.

  • Comparing two runs side by side, to show determinism visually rather than just claiming it, is still on my list.

I’m still learning Fiber, so corrections are genuinely welcome.

If you spot anything I’ve misunderstood, or have a failure scenario that would be useful to reproduce, I’d be happy to hear about it.

Thanks for taking a look

item.title: Zedify — Fiber Network-native commerce platform for emerging-market merchants
item.dc:creator: theiceeman
item.description:
Zedify is a merchant commerce platform giving small businesses — starting with food, fashion,
gadgets, and vehicle sellers — a ready-to-launch storefront with Fiber Network payments built in
from checkout, alongside fiat rails. Rather than requiring every merchant to commission custom
development, Zedify uses a template-based shop builder with owner-controlled theming and
checkout settings (including whether to accept pay-on-delivery), keeping delivery costs low
while still integrating a production Fiber Network Node for real, routed CKB/UDT settlement. The
storefront and dashboard are live today at wt-payments-frontend.vercel.app, backed by our
own production FNN node on CKB testnet. We’re requesting a grant to take this from a working testnet deployment to a mainnet-ready, audited product targeting first Nigeria, then broader emerging-market, merchant adoption.

Detailed Technical Specification
Problem:
Small merchants in markets like Nigeria face two compounding problems: e-commerce tooling
that’s either too expensive or too generic for their category of business, and payment
infrastructure built around card rails with high fees, slow settlement, and no protection against
local currency depreciation.
Solution
● A multi-category storefront template (food, fashion, gadgets, vehicles) with
category-aware product attributes, so merchants get a working store without bespoke
development
● Fiber Network integrated as a first-class checkout option alongside fiat, generating real
invoices against our own production FNN node
● A stablecoin savings feature routing fiat deposits into RUSD (Fiber/CKB-native), USDT,
or USDC — giving users a Fiber-native option for preserving value against currency
depreciation, extending RUSD’s exposure to a mainstream non-crypto-native audience

Architecture:
● Backend: AdonisJS 5 (TypeScript), PostgreSQL/Lucid ORM, deployed on Render
● Frontend: Next.js, deployed on Vercel — live storefront and merchant dashboard, not
just a repo

● Fiber integration: fiber-rpc-js against a self-hosted, production FNN node (v0.9.1),
running persistently via systemd with Biscuit-scoped RPC authentication
● Payment detection: a dedicated polling path (PaymentIndexerService) that queries
our own node’s invoice/payment status directly — correct for Fiber’s off-chain settlement
model, rather than watching an on-chain indexer the way our EVM rail does
Current status (testnet, verified)
● Live merchant storefront and dashboard deployed and publicly reachable at
wt-payments-frontend.vercel.app, wired end-to-end to the backend below — not just a
local demo
● Production FNN node funded, peered with public testnet bootnodes, holding live
ChannelReady payment channels
● Real invoices generated through our own checkout API (not manual CLI), confirmed
structurally valid
● Multiple genuine routed payments between independent nodes settled with status:
Success, confirmed via get_payment
● RUSD configured as a supported settlement asset alongside USDT/USDC

Try it yourself:
If you run fnn-cli or an equivalent Fiber node, you can pay our live storefront for real, right
now:

  1. Connect to our node — peer address and pubkey are in the backend README.
  2. Visit wt-payments-frontend.vercel.app, add a product to cart, and choose Fiber at
    checkout to get a live fibt… invoice.
  3. Pay it: fnn-cli payment send_payment --invoice
  4. If routing fails with no path found, open a small direct channel to us (details in the
    README) — testnet liquidity can be uneven, but a direct channel guarantees a route.
  5. Confirm settlement with fnn-cli payment get_payment --payment-hash￼<payment_hash> — look for status: Success.
    Need testnet CKB first? The Nervos Pudge Faucet works.

Open items, stated plainly
● A fully external, judge/community-tested routed payment (infrastructure and instructions
are ready — see JUDGE_INSTRUCTIONS.md in the backend repo)
● Liquidity/on-ramp partner selection for the fiat→stablecoin conversion path
● Legal review of the custodial stablecoin savings feature ahead of handling real funds,
given it’s open to any platform user.

Links

● Live storefront & dashboard: www.wt-payments-frontend.vercel.app/
● Frontend repo: github.com/chukwuagoziesolomon/wt-payments--frontend-

● Backend repo: github.com/chukwuagoziesolomon/zedify-server-

We’d genuinely like community members to try the routed payment flow above and tell us where

it breaks.

item.title: Nervape Artist RGB++ DOB：基于 RGB++ 和 Bitcoin 的猴子链上认证与所有权方案
item.dc:creator: faber_yang
item.description:
Nervape Artist RGB++ DOB：基于 RGB++ 和 Bitcoin 的猴子链上认证与所有权方案

1. 方案概述

Artist RGB++ DOB 利用 RGB++ 与 Bitcoin 技术，为每只艺术家猴子建立可验证的链上身份和链上所有权。芯片提供实体身份凭证，RGB++ 连接 DOB 数据与 Bitcoin UTXO，Bitcoin 网络记录 DOB 的发行、所有权和转移结果。

链上认证以“实体芯片 → 芯片地址 → Bitcoin UTXO → RGB++ DOB”为验证链路；在 BTC 主状态下，链上所有权以 Bitcoin 网络中当前有效的 DOB UTXO 及其锁定地址为准。 CKB 作为 RGB++ 的数据与验证层，用于保存艺术家信息和 DOB 数据，并验证 Bitcoin UTXO 对应的资产状态。

  • RGB++ 将 CKB 侧 DOB 数据与 Bitcoin UTXO 建立同构绑定；
  • DOB 通过 Bitcoin 交易发行，Bitcoin UTXO 表达链上所有权；
  • 艺术家信息、DOB metadata、DNA 和渲染数据记录在 CKB 侧 DOB Cell 中；
  • 用户通过芯片验证完成认领，DOB mint 到猴子芯片生成的 Bitcoin 地址，Nervape 记录当前实体持有人；
  • DOB 在 CKB 与 BTC 之间的迁移通过 RGB++ leap 完成。

2. 涉及到的对象和关系

2.1 CKB Artist DOB Cell

CKB Artist DOB Cell 是艺术家 DOB 的数据载体，主要记录：

  • Artist DOB 唯一标识；
  • 艺术家相关信息；
  • RGB++ 绑定所需的状态信息。

2.2 BTC DOB UTXO

BTC DOB UTXO 是 Artist RGB++ DOB 在 Bitcoin 网络上的所有权凭证，主要用于：

  • 表达 DOB 在 Bitcoin 网络上的所有权状态；
  • 接收 Bitcoin 网络上的 mint；
  • 参与 RGB++ leap。

2.3 猴子芯片地址

每只艺术家猴子的芯片生成独立 BTC 地址。该地址用于接收RGB++ DOB 的UTXO，是实体身份与 Bitcoin 链上所有权之间的连接点。

2.4 Nervape 实体持有人

Nervape 记录当前实体猴子的持有人，由用户完成芯片验证后建立或更新。该记录用于实体交付和产品服务，不替代 Bitcoin UTXO 表达的链上所有权。

2.5 关系图

flowchart TB
  artist[艺术家 / 发行方] --> artistData[艺术家信息]
  artistData --> dobCell[CKB Artist DOB Cell]
  dobCell --> dobType[DOB Type Script 验证]
  dobCell <--> binding[RGB++ 同构绑定]

  monkey[艺术家猴子实体] --> chip[安全芯片]
  chip --> chipAddress[芯片 Bitcoin 地址]
  chipAddress --> dobUtxo[Bitcoin DOB UTXO]
  binding <--> dobUtxo
  dobUtxo --> ownership[链上所有权]

  chip --> claim[芯片验证与认领]
  claim --> holder[Nervape 实体持有人]

3. 实现原理

3.1 艺术家猴子链上认证原理

每只艺术家猴子的芯片身份、芯片生成的 Bitcoin 地址、BTC DOB UTXO 和 CKB Artist DOB Cell 组成唯一认证链路。验证者通过芯片挑战响应确认实体芯片，再沿 RGB++ 绑定关系查询 DOB 数据和 Bitcoin UTXO 状态，从而验证猴子实体及其链上 DOB 的真实性。链上认证成立需要同时满足芯片验证有效、BTC DOB UTXO 未被消费、RGB++ 绑定有效，以及 CKB DOB 数据与芯片标识一致。

3.2 链上所有权原理

当 Artist RGB++ DOB 位于 Bitcoin 网络时，其链上所有权由 UTXO 模型表达。当前未花费的 BTC DOB UTXO 是所有权凭证，其锁定地址是当前链上所有者。RGB++ 将每次 Bitcoin 所有权变化同步到 CKB DOB Cell 的绑定状态，使链上所有权与 DOB 数据保持一致。

3.3 Bitcoin 网络作为主执行层

Artist RGB++ DOB 的资产操作以 Bitcoin UTXO 为基础。发行时创建绑定到芯片地址的 BTC DOB UTXO。CKB 不代替 Bitcoin 执行资产转移。CKB 侧保存 DOB 数据，并通过 RGB++ 规则验证和同步 Bitcoin 网络上的 UTXO 状态。

3.4 CKB 侧记录 DOB 数据

发行方首先在 CKB 创建 Artist DOB Cell。DOB Type Script 约束 DOB 数据格式和状态变更规则，Cell data 保存艺术家信息、metadata、DNA 与渲染数据。

3.5 RGB++ 建立同构绑定

RGB++ 协议将 CKB Artist DOB Cell 与 BTC UTXO 建立绑定。BTC UTXO 发生合法变更后，CKB 侧根据 RGB++ 规则验证对应的 BTC 交易，并将 DOB 状态同步到新的绑定关系。

3.6 Bitcoin 网络发行

Artist RGB++ DOB 通过 Bitcoin 交易发行，所有者固定为猴子芯片生成的 Bitcoin 地址。

准备 Artist DOB 数据
→ 创建 CKB Artist DOB Cell
→ 获取猴子芯片 Bitcoin 地址
→ 构造 RGB++ mint 交易
→ 在 Bitcoin 网络创建 DOB UTXO
→ 将 DOB UTXO 绑定到芯片地址
→ 等待 BTC 与 CKB 状态确认

发行完成后，DOB ID、CKB Cell、BTC UTXO 和芯片唯一标识需要形成可查询的映射关系。

3.7 芯片认领

用户认领时不改变 BTC DOB UTXO，也不将 DOB 转入用户钱包。认领过程通过芯片签名或挑战响应验证实体在场，并在 Nervape 登记当前实体持有人。链上所有权仍由锁定到芯片地址的 BTC DOB UTXO 表达。认领记录至少包含 DOB ID、芯片唯一标识、用户 ID、验证时间和当前状态。

3.8 实体持有人变更

实体猴子转手后，新持有人重新完成芯片验证。验证成功后，Nervape 更新实体持有人记录，RGB++ DOB 的链上所有权仍由芯片地址持有的 BTC DOB UTXO 表达，不触发 Bitcoin 链上交易。

4. 跨链方案

4.1 BTC 到 CKB

BTC 到 CKB 使用 RGB++ leap特性，将 BTC UTXO 表达的 DOB 持有状态切换为 CKB DOB Cell 持有状态。

选择 BTC DOB UTXO
→ 指定目标 CKB 地址，即芯片CKB地址
→ 构造 BTC -> CKB leap 交易
→ 完成 BTC 侧签名并广播
→ 提交 CKB 侧 RGB++ 交易
→ RGB++ 校验 BTC 交易状态
→ DOB Cell 绑定到目标 CKB owner lock
→ CKB 地址持有 Artist RGB++ DOB

4.2 CKB 到 BTC

CKB 到 BTC 使用 RGB++ leap特性，将 CKB 地址控制的 Artist DOB Cell 切换为目标 BTC UTXO 持有。

选择 CKB Artist DOB Cell
→ 指定目标 BTC 地址，即芯片的BTC地址
→ 构造 CKB -> BTC leap 交易
→ 提交 CKB 交易
→ 在 BTC 创建目标 DOB UTXO
→ RGB++ 校验并建立新绑定
→ BTC 地址持有 Artist RGB++ DOB UTXO

4.3 跨链图示

flowchart TB
  subgraph BTC[Bitcoin 网络]
    direction TB
    btcOwner[芯片 Bitcoin 地址]
    btcUtxo[BTC DOB UTXO]
    btcOwner --> btcUtxo
  end

  subgraph RGBPP[RGB++ Leap]
    direction TB

5. 总结

Nervape Artist RGB++ DOB 利用 RGB++ 和 Bitcoin 技术，为艺术家猴子建立“实体身份、链上数据与链上所有权”一体化的认证关系。

  • 安全芯片为每只艺术家猴子提供唯一身份，并生成用于接收 RGB++ DOB 的 Bitcoin 地址；
  • CKB Artist DOB Cell 记录艺术家信息和 DOB 数据；
  • RGB++ 将 CKB DOB Cell 与 Bitcoin UTXO 建立绑定，使实体猴子、DOB 数据和链上资产能够相互验证；
  • Bitcoin UTXO 作为链上所有权凭证，其锁定地址表示当前链上所有者；
  • 用户通过验证芯片完成认领，Nervape 记录当前实体持有人，认领过程不改变 Bitcoin UTXO 的所有权状态；
  • RGB++ leap 支持 DOB 在 Bitcoin 与 CKB 之间迁移，并保持 DOB 数据与链上持有状态一致。

该方案以 Bitcoin 网络承载 Artist RGB++ DOB 的发行和链上所有权，以 RGB++ 连接 Bitcoin UTXO 与 CKB DOB 数据，以安全芯片完成实体猴子的身份认证，从而形成可验证、可查询、可跨链的艺术家猴子链上认证体系。
